entries.title: Developer Guide
entries.content:
Developer Guide

Welcome to the CrowdVision Developer Guide. CrowdVision is a real-time crowd monitoring platform built on a digital twin: it streams live IoT sensor data into a 3D model of each building, for the people who manage those facilities.

Core paradigm
-----
Every service owns one bounded context and its own database. Services talk through their APIs and broker events, so telemetry, the twin and alerts can each change on their own.

System Capabilities

CrowdVision

- Digital Twin
	- 3D spatial building model
- Telemetry Ingestion
	- Sensor readings, thresholds
- Telemetry Distribution
	- Per-building live streams
- Alerting & Safety
	- Threshold breaches, Web Push
- Identity & Access
	- OIDC, memberships, Cedar
- Knowledge Assistant
	- RAG over this guide
- Simulators
	- Synthetic telemetry

Domain Responsibilities

Each bounded context runs on its own and exchanges events with the others.

Telemetry Ingestion

Takes one batch per building tick, checks thresholds and publishes raw readings.

Rust + Kafka

Digital Twin

Holds the spatial model of each building and estimates Wi-Fi device positions.

Rust + MongoDB

Alerting

Consumes threshold breaches, dedupes them on a cooldown and delivers Web Push.

Rust + Redis

Identity & Tenancy

Exchanges Keycloak tokens, mints the internal JWT and evaluates access policy.

Go + Cedar

Ready to start building?

Set up the stack, then explore the APIs: Setting up the environment · OpenAPI spec

entries.title: API Reference
entries.content:
API Reference

Every service’s edge surface: HTTP as OpenAPI 3 (rendered by Swagger UI), the Socket.IO feed as AsyncAPI 3. The specs are sources in this repository, at api/*.yaml, and are published alongside this guide — so a spec change ships in the same commit as the handler it describes. They document the edge-facing surface only: internal service-to-service hops and cross-boundary payload shapes are contracts in schemas/, not public APIs.

Gateway API

claims-gateway: Keycloak login and token exchange, the session cookie, /verify for the edge.

gateway.yaml

Tenancy API

tenancy: domains, subdomains, memberships and invite codes.

tenancy.yaml

Twin API

digital-twin: building upload and status, per-domain reads, sensor placements.

twin.yaml

Telemetry API

telemetry: batch ingest, sensors, thresholds, device actions, simulation.

telemetry.yaml

Dashboard API

dashboard: the metric catalog and each building’s column preferences.

dashboard.yaml

Notification API

notification: Web Push subscriptions, alert switches, manual alerts.

notification.yaml

Chat API

chat: conversations, and answers streamed as Server-Sent Events.

chat.yaml

Agent API

agent: ask the assistant, ingest documents. Generated from the FastAPI app.

agent.yaml

Socket API

socket: the live Socket.IO feed — notifications, telemetry ticks, device dots, building subscriptions.

socket.yaml · AsyncAPI

Common Error Responses

The error bodies each stack sends, referenced by the specs above.

error.yaml

socket.yaml is AsyncAPI 3, not OpenAPI: Socket.IO pushes events instead of answering requests, so it opens in its own viewer (api/asyncapi.html). registry and provisioner have no edge route, so they have no card.

entries.title: Coverage
entries.content:
Coverage

Line and branch coverage per service, read live from the coverage-data branch. cd-coverage.yml recomputes it on every push to master — for changed services only — and force-pushes summary.json, badge.json and coverage-counts.json to that orphan branch. Nothing is committed to master, so this page is always the branch’s current state, not a snapshot taken at docs-build time.

Coverage is produced per language by tpl-{rust,go,node,python}-coverage.yml. Bands match the badge thresholds in scripts/coverage-summary.py: 80% and above is healthy, 60% to 80% needs attention, below 60% is thin. Services are ordered by line coverage, weakest last. Branch coverage is only reported where the language’s tooling emits it.

Click a service to open its report under the row: every file, the ones with the most never-run lines first. Open a file to see those lines as ranges, each a link to the exact lines on GitHub at the commit that was measured. The report comes from the tool’s own line-level output (lcov.info for Rust and the frontend, coverage.xml for Go and Python), stored as reports/<service>.json on the same branch. Files from shared crates or libraries compiled into a service’s tests are left out of its report: they have their own row.

-----

Current coverage

entries.title: The Whole Picture
entries.content:
The Whole Picture

OrganizationTenantTwinReadingLimitBreachAlertPassNewsWordA customerSame as Organization, used when talking about keeping data apartThe 3D copy of a real buildingOne value from one room at one momentThe range a value should stay inThe time a room spends outside a limitThe message sent for one BreachStatement of who you are and your memberships“This happened”, sent to whoever listensMeaningnorthfield-universityNorthfield and AcmeThe 3D Science HallLab 2, 14:05, 27 °C18 to 26 °CLab 2, from 14:05 to 14:20“Lab 2 is too hot”Lia’s passBreach StartedExample

Two words to keep apart
-----
- Domain in this chapter: one area of the business, like Alerting. The six are listed below.
- Organization: a customer, like a university. The rest of the guide and the code call this a “Domain” too. Here it is always “Organization”.

-----

The story, in six questions

Everything comes from six questions. Each one needs the answers before it, so the order is not random.

123456#Who are you, and what may you do?What does the place look like?What is happening in each room, and is it OK?How do people follow a building, live?Who must be told, and where?Can someone explain all this to me?QuestionIdentity & AccessBuilding ManagementTelemetry IngestionTelemetry DistributionAlertingKnowledge & AssistanceDomainNothing1, to know whose building it is2, a reading needs a room3, something to follow1, 2 and 31, 2 and 3Needs

Click through the map, or read the pages in this order.

CrowdVision

- 1. Identity & Access
	- Who are you?
- 2. Building Management
	- What does the place look like?
- 3. Telemetry Ingestion
	- What is happening? Is it OK?
- 4. Telemetry Distribution
	- How do people follow it?
- 5. Alerting
	- Who must be told?
- 6. Knowledge & Assistance
	- Can you explain it?

-----

How the domains talk

Three ways, and only three.

- The pass. Identity & Access gives each person a pass: who they are, and their role in each organization. Every domain trusts it.
- News. A domain says “this happened” and does not care who listens.
- A question. One domain asks another for something only that domain knows.



Solid arrow: news. Dotted arrow: a question. Identity & Access is left out because everyone holds its pass.

All the news

Building ReadyReading RecordedBreach StartedBreach EndedNewsBuilding ManagementTelemetry IngestionTelemetry IngestionTelemetry IngestionSaid byIngestion, DistributionDistributionAlerting, DistributionDistributionHeard bySet starting limits, set starting FocusUpdate the building’s statusTell people, mark the roomMark the room as back to normalWhat the listener does

All the questions

AlertingKnowledge & AssistanceKnowledge & AssistanceWho asksBuilding ManagementBuilding ManagementTelemetry IngestionWho answersWhich organizations own this building?What is this building?What is happening right now?QuestionOwnership is a Building Management fact, and an alert must never reach the wrong tenantThe assistant owns no factsSameWhy ask

-----

One full example

Made-up numbers, used on every page of this chapter.

- Organization: northfield-university
- Building: Science Hall
- Room: Lab 2, temperature limit 18 to 26 °C
- People: Ada (Domain Administrator), Sam (Staff Member), Lia (Standard User)

Sam has a phone and a tablet. At 14:00 the lab is 25 °C. At 14:05 it reaches 27 °C.



What to notice:

- Ingestion knows about the limit, not about Sam.
- Alerting knows about Sam, not about what 26 °C means.
- Following a building and being told are separate. Sam is told even if nobody is following.
- 14:05 and 14:10 are two readings but one problem, so one alert.

-----

Rules that hold everywhere

1. One owner per fact. A room’s size lives in Building Management. Its temperature lives in Telemetry Ingestion. Nobody keeps their own copy of the truth.
2. An organization is known by its name. The name is the only thing all domains share.
3. Tenants never see each other. This holds in every domain.
4. What happened stays recorded. A wrong reading is fixed by a new reading, never by an edit.

-----

How much care each domain gets

Not every domain deserves the same effort.

CoreSupportingKindThe reason customers payNeeded, but nobody picks us for itMeaningBuilding Management, Telemetry Ingestion, Telemetry DistributionIdentity & Access, Alerting, Knowledge & AssistanceDomains

-----

Not in this model

Left out for now:

- Sending commands to devices, like turning a boiler up.
- Knowing where each person is inside a building.
- Billing and subscriptions.

headings.text: How much care each domain gets

entries.title: Identity & Access
entries.content:
Identity & Access

AccountOrganizationSub-organizationMembershipRoleSign-in MethodPassTenantWordOne person who can sign inA customer. The unit that keeps data apartA part of an organization with its own access“This person belongs here, with this role”How much a person may do inside one organizationHow an organization checks peopleStatement of who you are and your membershipsSame as Organization: one customer, kept apart from the othersMeaningLianorthfield-universityphysics under NorthfieldLia in Northfield, Standard UserStaff MemberIts own passwords, or the company loginLia’s pass, valid for minutesNorthfield and Acme are two tenantsExample

Question: who are you, and what may you do? Kind: Supporting. Needs: nothing.

Comes first because every other domain needs to know who is asking.

-----

In the real world

Lia studies at Northfield University and volunteers at a city museum. Both use CrowdVision.

- She should not need two logins.
- At the university she is a Standard User. At the museum she is Staff.
- The two must never mix.

So: a person is one thing, and their place inside an organization is another.

-----

The model



-----

Roles

Three roles. Each can do everything the one below can.

	Domain Administrator > Staff Member > Standard User

Standard UserStaff MemberDomain AdministratorRoleSee buildings and live values, ask the assistantAlso edit rooms, connect sensors, set room limitsAlso add buildings, onboard members, split the organizationCan

Checking is one rule: your role must be at least the one needed.

The Platform Administrator is not on this list. They run the platform and hold no membership.

-----

Rules

1. One Account has at most one Membership per Organization. Joining again changes the role. It does not add a second one.
2. An Organization’s name is unique and never changes. Everyone refers to it by that name.
3. An administrator can give a role up to their own, never higher.
4. Creating an Organization needs no human help: sign up, create, use.
5. A taken name is refused, and nothing is created.
6. An Organization using a company login takes no self-service joins. The company decides who is in.
7. A hidden Organization does not show in search. To outsiders, it does not exist.

-----

The pass

The main thing this domain gives to the others.

	who:          lia@example.com
	memberships:  northfield-university  Standard User
	              city-museum            Staff Member
	valid for:    a short time
	issued by:    Identity & Access, and nobody else

- Every domain trusts it and decides alone what its holder may do.
- Switching organization needs no new sign-in: the pass lists them all.
- Expired pass: sign in again. Never a silent yes.



Trade-off: if Lia loses a role, her pass still shows the old one until it expires. That is why a pass lives only for minutes.

-----

Open questions

- How deep can sub-organizations go? One level covers campus and department.
- Does a member of the parent see a sub-organization, or must they be added?

entries.title: Building Management
entries.content:
Building Management

BuildingBuilding DescriptionFloorRoomPositionSizeCapacityHighlightTwinOrganizationPassWordOne real structureWhat a person provides so a twin can be madeOne level of a buildingA bounded space on a floorWhere a room sits, as x, y, zWidth, height, depthHow many people a room is meant forA mark making a room stand outThe 3D copy of a real buildingA customer, the owner of buildingsStatement of who you are and your membershipsMeaningScience HallScience Hall: three floors, 40 roomsFloor 2Lab 212, 4, 610 by 3 by 8 m30Exam room this weekThe 3D Science Hallnorthfield-universityLia’s pass lists NorthfieldExample

Question: what does the place look like? Kind: Core. Needs: Identity & Access, to know whose building it is.

The 3D twin is the product. Everything live is drawn on top of this model.

-----

In the real world

Ada runs facilities at Northfield. She has a description of Science Hall: three floors, 40 rooms, where each room is and how big.

- She provides it and wants a twin, without a developer.
- A room is a place, not a measurement. Lab 2 stays Lab 2 at any temperature.
- The city owns the sports hall with the university. Both should see it, and it should exist once.

-----

The model



- A Room has no life of its own. It is created and changed through its Building.
- Position and Size are just values. No identity: 10 by 3 by 8 m is the same anywhere.
- Temperature is not on the Room. A room is a place. A temperature is something happening in it, and that is another domain’s question.

-----

From description to twin



- All or nothing. One bad room refuses the whole description. No half building.
- Valid does not mean finished. Accepted is a promise. Ready means the twin exists.

Example of a refusal:

	Ada describes Science Hall
	Room "Lab 2" has width -10
	Refused: room "Lab 2": width must be above 0
	Result: no building

-----

Rules

1. A Building belongs to one or more Organizations, by name.
2. A shared Building exists once. Two organizations see the same one.
3. You see a Building only if it belongs to one of the organizations on your pass.
4. The twin matches the real building: each Room at its real Position and Size.
5. Each Room belongs to one Floor.

Rule 3 needs only the pass:

	Lia's pass says:           northfield-university
	Science Hall belongs to:   northfield-university, city-of-northfield
	Overlap?                   yes, so she sees it
	Harbour Tower belongs to:  acme
	Overlap?                   no, so she does not

-----

What leaves this domain

Building Ready, with its roomsWhich organizations own a buildingWhat a building looks likeWhatNewsAnswer to a questionAnswer to a questionHowIngestion sets starting limits, Distribution sets starting FocusAlertingKnowledge & AssistanceTo whom

A building exists on its own. It does not depend on its limits or its Focus.

-----

Open questions

- What happens to a room’s limits and history when the room is deleted?
- Can a building lose its last organization?

entries.title: Telemetry Ingestion
entries.content:
Telemetry Ingestion

SensorMetricReadingLimitLimit SetBreachWindowBuilding ReadyWordA device connected to a roomA kind of thing we measureOne value from one room at one momentThe range a metric should stay inAll the limits of one buildingThe time a room spends outside a limitA time range for looking at historyNews that a new building can be usedMeaningThermometer T-204 in Lab 2TemperatureLab 2, 14:05, 27 °C18 to 26 °CScience Hall’s limitsLab 2, from 14:05 to 14:20Last weekScience Hall is readyExample

Question: what is happening in each room, and is it OK? Kind: Core. Needs: Building Management, a reading needs a room.

Turns noise from devices into facts the platform can trust.

-----

In the real world

Lab 2 has a thermometer. Every few seconds it says a number.

- Some numbers are garbage, or come from a device nobody connected.
- Good numbers must be kept: after an incident, people ask what really happened.
- A number means little alone. 27 °C is fine in a corridor and bad in a server room.

So three jobs: check it, keep it, judge it.

-----

The model



-----

A reading’s path



Rejected readings never enter the platform. The sender is told why, so a broken device can be found.

-----

Which limit applies?

The room’s own limit wins. Otherwise the building’s.

Lab 2CorridorRoom18 to 26noneOwn limit16 to 2816 to 28Building limit18 to 2616 to 28Limit used2727ReadingBreachOKVerdict

A building has exactly one Limit Set. A new one replaces the old, so nobody asks which limit was active.

-----

One breach, many readings

A breach is a period, not a reading. This is what makes “one problem, one alert” true.

14:0014:0514:1014:1514:20Time252727.526.525ValueInsideAboveAboveAboveInsideLimit 18 to 26NoneStartsStill openStill openEndsBreachBreach StartedBreach EndedNews



Why here, and not in Alerting? Whether 27 °C is bad depends on the room, and that is this domain’s knowledge. Who hears about it is about people. That is Alerting’s.

-----

Rules

1. Only a connected Sensor is listened to. Disconnect it and its next reading is rejected.
2. A Reading is never changed or deleted. A correction is a new Reading.
3. A Reading says which building, which room, and when. Missing one means rejected.
4. Each Metric has a name and a unit.

-----

How a metric describes itself

	name:  Temperature
	unit:  °C

Telemetry Distribution collects these into its catalog. Describe Noise tomorrow and people can pick it right away.

-----

Looking back

History comes from recorded readings.

	Lab 2, temperature, Monday, average over the day
	Readings:  22, 24, 27, 23
	Average:   24 °C

-----

What leaves this domain

Reading RecordedBreach StartedBreach EndedMetric descriptionsCurrent values and limitsWhatNewsNewsNewsShared listAnswer to a questionHowDistributionAlerting, DistributionDistributionDistributionKnowledge & AssistanceTo whom

-----

Open questions

- A silent sensor: is no reading for an hour a problem? There is no story yet.
- A limit changes during a breach: judged again at the next reading?
- What are the starting limits for a new building?

entries.title: Telemetry Distribution
entries.content:
Telemetry Distribution

Building StatusLatest ValueMetric CatalogFocusReadingTwinWordThe state of every room of a building, right nowThe newest reading of a metric in a roomEverything that can be measuredThe metrics a building compares its rooms on, most important firstOne value from one room at one momentThe 3D copy of a real buildingMeaningScience Hall at 14:05Lab 2, 27 °CTemperature, People, CapacityTemperature, then PeopleLab 2, 14:05, 27 °CThe 3D Science HallExample

Question: how do people follow a building, live? Kind: Core. Needs: Telemetry Ingestion, something to follow.

Readings exist. Now each person has to be able to follow them, in a way that fits their work.

-----

In the real world

Sam looks after Science Hall from the facilities office.

- 40 rooms, and Sam needs to spot the odd one out.
- Sam cares about temperature and people, not air quality.
- What Sam knows must always be now.

-----

The model



Importance is part of the model. What matters most comes first.

-----

The catalog is collected, not invented

Each domain describes what it owns. This domain just gathers them.



A new metric can be picked as soon as its owner describes it.

-----

Two separate things

This is the idea to remember.

HoldsDecided byUsed forEvery metric of every roomWhat really happensEverything that shows the buildingBuilding StatusOnly the chosen metricsPeopleComparing roomsFocus

Example. Ada removes Temperature from the Focus. The 3D twin still colours Lab 2 by temperature, because the status still knows it. The Focus changes what is compared, not what is known.



-----

Rules

1. A reading changes the status of its own building, and no other.
2. Every room of the building can be compared, on its Latest Values.
3. A room with no reading has no value, which is not 0. Zero people is a real value.
4. A new building already has a Focus. Nobody has to set one up first.
5. Only people whose pass allows the building can follow it.

-----

Staying current

A person must never take an old value for the current one.

	14:04  Sam stops following. Last value: 25 °C.
	14:05  Reading: 27 °C. Sam misses it.
	14:07  Sam is back. Sam knows 27 °C.

Missed readings do not matter one by one. Only now matters here. The past lives in Telemetry Ingestion.

-----

Open questions

- One Focus per building, or one per person?
- What is the starting Focus of a new building?
- Does a room in breach need to stand out, or is the value alone enough?

headings.text: The catalog is collected, not invented

entries.title: Alerting
entries.content:
Alerting

AlertAlert TypeAlert ChoiceDeviceRecipientBreachOpt inWordThe message sent for one BreachA kind of alertWhat one person wants, in one organizationOne place a person can be reachedA person who gets this alertThe time a room spends outside a limitChoosing to receive somethingMeaning“Lab 2 is too hot”TemperatureSam, Northfield: temperature yes, air noSam’s phoneSamLab 2, from 14:05 to 14:20Sam opted in to temperature alertsExample

Question: who must be told, and where? Kind: Supporting. Needs: Identity & Access, Building Management, Telemetry Ingestion.

This domain never decides that something is wrong. Ingestion did that already. It only gets the news to the right people.

-----

In the real world

Lab 2 is too hot. Sam should hear about it, on the phone, even when not following the building.

Two different questions hide here:

- What does Sam want to hear about?
- Where can Sam be reached?

They change separately. A new phone must not reset Sam’s choices.

-----

The model



Device and Alert Choice are two separate things on purpose. Each one can be replaced without touching the other.

-----

Who gets it

Each step narrows the list. Numbers are made up.



The first step is the one question this domain asks: “which organizations own this building?”. Ownership is a Building Management fact.

-----

Worked example

SamAdaLiaMaxPersonNorthfieldNorthfieldNorthfieldAcmeMember?YesNoYesYesChose temperature?Phone, tabletPhoneNonePhoneDevicesYes, on bothNoNo, nowhere to send itNo, wrong organizationGets it?

Lia can see the problem by following the building. Alerts add to that, they do not replace it.

-----

Rules

1. One Breach, one Alert. Readings during the same breach send nothing new.
2. Only members of the building’s organizations, and only those who opted in.
3. A person has one Alert Choice per organization. Choices do not leak across.
4. An Alert goes to all of a person’s devices.
5. Removing a device keeps the choices and the other devices.

Edge case: shared building. Science Hall belongs to two organizations, and Sam is in both. Sam gets one alert, not two. It is one breach.

Edge case: back to normal. The room recovers before anyone reacts. Nothing extra is sent. No “ignore that” message.

-----

Open questions

- Does anyone need to acknowledge an alert?
- If nobody opted in, is it fine that nobody hears?
- A new member: are alerts on or off at the start? Alerts need an opt in, so off.

entries.title: Knowledge & Assistance
entries.content:
Knowledge & Assistance

InquiryConsultationSourceAnswerCitationPassGroundedWordOne question from one personLooking things up to answer one InquirySomething that can be looked atThe reply to one InquiryA pointer from a claim to its SourceStatement of who you are and your membershipsBacked by a Source that was really looked atMeaning“Is Lab 2 too hot?”Reading Lab 2’s temperature and limitA guide page, a live value“Yes, 27 °C, limit 26”“Live reading, 14:05”Sam’s pass lists Northfield“27 °C”, from a live readingExample

Question: can someone explain all this to me? Kind: Supporting. Needs: Identity & Access, Building Management, Telemetry Ingestion.

Ask in plain words, get an answer you can check. The rule above all: a wrong answer is worse than no answer.

-----

In the real world

Sam, walking down a corridor: “is the west wing still too hot?”

- Sam does not want to go looking for it.
- Sam will act on the answer, so it must be checkable.
- If the assistant does not know, it has to say so.

-----

The model



An Answer means nothing without its Inquiry, so they live together. A Source is maintained on its own, so it stands apart.

-----

Answering



The filter comes first. What the assistant cannot read, it cannot leak.

-----

Three answers

Is Lab 2 too hot?Why is Lab 2 hot?Is Harbour Tower OK?Sam asksReading 27 °C, limit 26Reading only, no causeNothing, Sam has no accessWhat was found“Yes, 27 °C, above the 26 °C limit.” With citations“It is 27 °C. I can’t tell why.”“I don’t know.”Answer

The third answer does not say “you have no access”. Even that would confirm the building exists.

-----

Rules

1. Every claim has a citation. No citation, no claim.
2. A citation can only point to something actually looked at.
3. “I don’t know” is a normal answer, not a failure.
4. Partial evidence means saying so, not sounding sure.
5. Only data from the person’s own organizations.
6. Every Inquiry gets an Answer, even a confusing one.
7. Questions about now use current values.
8. One Inquiry, one Answer. A follow-up is a new Inquiry.

-----

What it does not own

Nothing here is a fact about the world. Buildings stay in Building Management, readings stay in Telemetry Ingestion. This domain asks them, changes nothing, and turns the answer into its own words.

Nobody depends on this domain.

-----

Open questions

- Should it remember earlier questions in a conversation?
- Should it ever do things, or only answer? Today, only answer.
- Two Sources disagree: which wins?

entries.title: Architecture Overview
entries.content:
Architecture Overview

ServiceEdgeBrokerBounded contextCedarTenantControl planeWordA program deployed on its ownThe one door between the internet and the servicesA middleman that carries messagesOne domain, as owned by one or more servicesThe language CrowdVision’s access rules are written inOne customer organizationServices that run the platform, not the productMeaningtelemetryCaddy locally, Istio in the clusterRedis, KafkaAlerting is notificationpolicy.cedarNorthfieldregistry, provisionerExample

Six domains become twelve deployed parts. This page shows how, then how they run.

-----

From domain to services

Identity & AccessBuilding ManagementTelemetry IngestionTelemetry DistributionAlertingKnowledge & AssistanceDomainKeycloak, claims-gateway, tenancy, registry, provisionerdigital-twintelemetrydashboard, socketnotificationchat, agentServicesPostgreSQLMongoDBPostgreSQL + TimescaleDBMongoDB, socket has noneMongoDB, Redis for the cooldownMongoDB, PostgreSQL + pgvectorStore

Plus client, the Vue app everyone uses.

Why Identity needs four services:

- claims-gateway: answers “who is this?” on every sign-in.
- tenancy: remembers organizations and memberships.
- registry: takes a new customer’s signup.
- provisioner: turns a signup into a running organization.

A signup has no user yet, and a sign-in needs no new customer. They change for different reasons.

-----

The whole picture



Thin arrow: a request. Dotted: Redis, may be lost. Thick: Kafka, kept. To keep it readable this shows the main paths only. Communication & Data Flow lists every one.

-----

Rules of the structure

One database per service, never reach into another’sServices keep no sessionOne service, one domainHigh volume goes over a brokerEvery outbound HTTP call has a timeoutShapes that cross a service live in schemas/The frontend keeps state in composables and components; a global store only when several screens share itRuleA model cannot leak through shared tablesWho is asking travels with each requestA change stays in one placeA slow reader never holds back a sensorA hang gives no error, so no fallback runsTwo sides cannot drift apart unnoticedLess hidden state to reason aboutReason

A change that breaks one of these is rejected, even with CI green. Rules for how a change is made: Toolchain Overview.

-----

Same idea, different word

The domain speaks plainly. The code uses older names.

OrganizationPassLimitBreachFocusReadingDomainDomainJWT, x-gateway-claimsThresholdAlertEventBuilding preferences, columnsOne entry of a TelemetryEnvelopeCode

-----

Where code and domain disagree

The domain is right until someone decides otherwise. Each line is a to-do or a change to the domain.

One breach, one alertNews: Breach Started, Breach EndedStaff can edit roomsThree rolesStarting Focus comes from Building ReadyDomain saysOne alert per breaching reading, muted for 300 s per room and field. A long breach alerts every 5 minutesNo breach is kept, and nothing says it endedRooms are fixed at upload, there is no route to change themFour in roles.json: admin also existsdigital-twin calls dashboard directly, best effortCode does

-----

Shared code

Never deployed, always built into a service.

backend/libs/auth-contractsbackend/libs/auth-middlewarebackend/libs/auth-policyschemas/*-schemaschemas/fixtures, schemas/jsonFolderToken shape, role ladder, HMAC signingVerify a JWT, or read the edge’s headerThe one Cedar bundleRust crates for shared shapesExamples every language must parse, written contractsHoldsGo servicesclaims-gateway, tenancyEvery service that runs CedarRust servicesAllUsed by

-----

Two ways to run it

Started withEdgeChecks the tokenBetween servicesKeycloakjust stack devCaddyforward_auth to claims-gatewayPlain, on Docker networksIncludedLocaljust k8s createIstio gatewayRequestAuthentication at the gatewaymTLS, by ztunnelNot in these manifestsCluster

Same paths, same gates. Differences are listed in Trust & Service Mesh.

-----

Routes

Same table on both edges.

/gateway/tenancy/twin/telemetry/telemetry/ingest, /collector, /observations/dashboard/notification/chat/agent/socket.io/Pathclaims-gatewaytenancydigital-twintelemetrytelemetrydashboardnotificationchatagentsocketclientGoes toNo: client has no token yet, it gets one hereYesYesYesNo, signed with HMAC insteadYesYesYes, streams answers as SSENo, see TrustYesNoGated

registry and provisioner have no route: nothing outside may reach them.

Exact paths
-----
The three open telemetry paths are exact, and listed by hand on both edges. A sub-path falls under the gate and answers 401.

entries.title: Communication & Data Flow
entries.content:
Communication & Data Flow

TickPub/subTopicConsumer groupClaims headerHMACDead-letter topicWordEverything one building reports at one momentSend to whoever listens now; nobody listening, message goneA log that keeps messages until readReaders sharing one topic’s workWho the caller is, set by the edgeA signature proving a shared key was usedWhere messages that cannot be handled waitMeaningOne batch of readingsRedis channelKafka alertsalertsx-gateway-claimsX-Signaturealerts.dlqExample

How the services talk, and why each talk looks the way it does.

-----

Pick by what happens if the message is lost

HTTP with claimsHTTP with HMACRedis pub/subKafkaStyleA person is waitingNo person involved, like provisioningLive readings, in-app alertsBreaches, building registration, Wi-Fi ticksUsed forThe person sees an errorRetried on the next roundNothing: the next tick replaces itNot lost, read after a restartIf lost

Example. dashboard restarts for 10 seconds. Readings of those 10 seconds never reach its channel. Fine: a new tick comes, and a client that reconnects asks telemetry for the latest values. A breach in those 10 seconds waits in Kafka, because nothing else would remember it.

-----

Who is calling

A personA service acting for a personA service, no personA device or collectorCallerCookie with a JWTSame header, forwarded unchangedX-Signature, shared secretX-Signature, key of the buildingProofThe edge, once. Services read x-gateway-claimsThe receiving service, for what it allowsThe receivertelemetryChecked by

Full details: Trust & Service Mesh.

-----

Calls between services

digital-twindigital-twindigital-twinnotificationtelemetrysocketdashboardchatagentclaims-gatewayprovisionertelemetryFromtelemetrydashboardnotificationdigital-twindigital-twindigital-twintelemetry, digital-twinagentdigital-twin, telemetrytenancyregistry, tenancySimulatorsToPUT /thresholds/buildings/{id}POST /preferences/init/{id}POST /triggerGET /domain/{id}GET /domain/{id}GET /domain/{id}GET /contractsPOST /askRead routes/internal/memberships, /internal/provision/internal/.../control/*CallClaimsClaimsSystem claimsClaimsClaimsClaimsNoneClaimsClaimsHMACHMACNoneProofKeep the limit in step after an editStarting columns, best effortReport a failed provisioningWho owns this buildingWho may read this buildingMay this client subscribeCollect the metric catalogAnswer a question as that personTool calls, under the person’s own rightsOnce per sign-in, never per requestTurn a signup into an organizationStart and stop simulated buildingsWhy

registry and tenancy only receive. Only claims-gateway talks to Keycloak.

-----

Messages

Redis channels

telemetry:rawtelemetry:filtered:{buildingId}notificationstwin:devices:{buildingId}Channeltelemetrydashboardnotificationdigital-twinFromdashboardsocketsocketsocketToOne envelope per tickSame bytes, per buildingOne alert, for one organizationEstimated device dots, no ids, never storedCarries

Kafka topics

alertsalerts.dlqbuilding-registration-requestedbuilding-registration-completedwifi-observationsestimated-occupancyTopictelemetrynotificationdigital-twintelemetrytelemetrydigital-twinFromnotificationNobody yettelemetrydigital-twindigital-twintelemetryToalertsbuilding-registrationsbuilding-registrations-completedwifi-observationsestimated-occupancyGroupOne message per breach of a fieldAlerts that could not be handledNew building and its roomsready or failedReceived Wi-Fi ticks, kept 10 minRoom counts, stored as readingsCarries

All names come from schemas/, never typed by hand in a service.

Two services never share a group
-----
A group shares the work: each partition goes to one member. These topics have one partition, so in a shared group one service would read everything and the other nothing. Copies of one service do share a group.

Renaming a group replays the topic
-----
No saved position means reading from the start. Harmless for registration, since every write is an upsert. For alerts, old breaches go out again as real pushes, limited only by the cooldown. Wait for retention to pass, or move the new group to latest first.

-----

Flows

A reading reaches the screen



- One bad reading refuses the whole batch. At most 500 readings.
- 202 means stored, so the data can be queried.
- dashboard and socket pass the bytes on, unread. Columns are applied in the browser, so the 3D twin still gets every metric.

A breach reaches a person



- Same message, two roads: bell in the app, push outside it.
- The push road needs no open tab.
- Delivery can happen twice, so a Redis cooldown of 300 s absorbs repeats.
- Failed lookup: parked on alerts.dlq, cooldown not set.
- No owner: dropped, and counted.

A building is registered



- Validation runs before the answer, so a bad file is refused at once.
- Each side commits only after handling, and every write is an upsert. Repeats change nothing.
- resync sends the request again when telemetry lost a building.

Wi-Fi ticks



Bytes go on as received, and unknown fields are refused, so a stray MAC address cannot reach Kafka. Details: Wireless People Flow.

Sign-in



Later requests need no call to tenancy. The app renews every 10 minutes.

Signup



A 409 from tenancy counts as success, so a repeat is safe.

A question to the assistant



The same access rules apply as if the person had called directly. The assistant holds no rights of its own.

entries.title: Trust & Service Mesh
entries.content:
Trust & Service Mesh

Service meshmTLSWorkload identityztunnelClaims headerForgeWordA layer that secures traffic between services, outside their codeEncryption where both sides prove who they areThe mesh’s proof of which service is callingIstio’s per-node proxy, carries all trafficWho the person is, set by the edgeSend a made-up header to pose as someoneMeaningIstioBetween any two podschat’s accountOne per nodex-gateway-claimsA fake admin claimExample

Who is trusted, by whom, and where that stops.

-----

The idea: a hard shell

EdgeMeshServiceLayerIs this a real signed-in person?Is every hop encrypted, and from a real workload?May this person, in this organization, do this?QuestionIstio gateway, onceztunnel, PeerAuthentication: STRICTCedar, inside the serviceWhere



Why once: services hold no signing keys, and no request pays for checking twice.

-----

What this does not stop

A workload already inside the cluster can call a service directly and send a forged header. mTLS proves the connection, not the content.

- From outside: not possible. Services have no public address, and the gateway wants a JWT.
- agent: gets extra care, since it runs an LLM on untrusted text. Only the gateway and chat may reach it (k8s/istio-agent-authz.yml).
- Accepted for now.

When this must change
-----
This holds while one cluster serves one customer. With several tenants in one hosted cluster, one broken workload becomes a cross-tenant leak. Then each service needs its own ServiceAccount and an AuthorizationPolicy listing its callers, as agent has.

-----

Open doors

/gateway/telemetry/ingest, /collector, /observations/agent/grafana/Pathclient has no token before signing inDevices have no personThe eval runner has its own tokenIt has its own loginThe app itselfWhy openKeycloakHMAC with the building’s key, in telemetryThe edge removes any x-gateway-claims, and the policy aboveOnly that passwordNothing neededWhat guards it

Why /agent strips the header: the door is open, so nobody checked that header. agent would believe a forged one.

-----

Keys

Keycloak and claims-gatewayclaims-gateway and the edgeControl plane servicesDevices and telemetryBetweenOIDCRS256, public keys at JWKSShared HMAC secretHMAC, derived per buildingKeyOnly claims-gateway talks to KeycloakOnly claims-gateway signsOne implementation, in auth-contractsRevoke by bumping an epoch. Separate key: this one leaves for customer sitesNote

-----

Why Istio, why ambient

- Istio, not Linkerd: Linkerd cannot validate a person’s JWT. Istio’s stable releases are also free.
- Ambient, not sidecars: sensors send a lot of data. ztunnel only does L4, so nothing parses bulk traffic. Parsing stays at the edge, where decisions are made.

Measured on a single dev node: Redis p50 stays under 5 ms inside the mesh.

-----

Known traps

istiod cannot fetch JWKS from a STRICT pod
-----
istiod is outside the mesh, so ztunnel refuses its plain request. jwksUri goes through the gateway’s own route instead.

Naming a JWT location replaces the defaults
-----
fromHeaders or fromCookies on a jwtRule turns off Authorization: Bearer. List both: browsers use the cookie, others the header.

A wildcard misses the bare path
-----
Istio’s /twin/* does not match /twin, but the route does. Every protected service is listed in both forms.

Keycloak ignores a changed realm file
-----
--import-realm skips a realm that exists. After changing keycloak/realm-export.json, delete the keycloak_postgres_data volume and let it import again.

-----

Local vs cluster

Same gated paths. Local only:

- Vite dev server for the app.
- Mongo Express GUIs at /*-db-gui.
- Prometheus through the edge. In the cluster it stays inside.

Simulators are never deployed to the cluster. They post to /telemetry/ingest like any device.

-----

Before real production

The manifests give a working cluster. These inputs cannot live in the repository:

HTTPSKeycloakImage accessReal secretsModel keyStrong Grafana passwordNeededThe gateway listens on plain :80Not in these manifests:latest with IfNotPresent. Use fixed tagsscripts/k8s/k8s-secrets.sh makes dev onesagent starts without OPENROUTER_API_KEY, then fails each requestIt is the only guard thereToday

entries.title: Deployment & Kubernetes
entries.content:
Deployment & Kubernetes

PodDeploymentStatefulSetPVCInit containerk3dWordOne running copy of a serviceKeeps stateless pods runningSame, for pods with their own diskA disk claimed by a podRuns first, must finish before the service startsKubernetes in Docker, for local useMeaningtelemetry-5d8...k8s/deployments/chat.ymltwin-db-0twin-data-twin-db-0wait-for-dbjust k8s createExample

How the cluster is built. Commands and setup: Kubernetes & Istio.

-----

What is in k8s/

	k8s/
	├── namespace.yml                     # crowdvision, enrolled in ambient mode
	├── istio-gateway.yml                 # the gateway and one route per service
	├── istio-peer-authentication.yml     # STRICT mTLS
	├── istio-request-authentication.yml  # JWT check at the edge
	├── istio-agent-authz.yml             # who may call agent
	├── configmaps/common.yml             # shared settings that are not secret
	├── deployments/                      # 12 stateless services
	├── stateful/                         # 8 databases, Redis, Kafka
	└── monitoring/                       # Prometheus, Grafana

-----

Stateless or stateful

DeploymentStatefulSetKindThe 12 services4 MongoDB, 4 PostgreSQL, Redis, KafkaWhatA new one starts anywhereSame name, same diskIf a pod dies



-----

Starting order

A service must not start before its database. Each pod waits in an init container:

	initContainers:
	  - name: wait-for-db
	    image: busybox:1.38.0
	    command: [sh, -c, "until nc -z twin-db 27017; do sleep 2; done"]

- provisioner also waits for registry and tenancy.
- claims-gateway waits for tenancy.
- The check only proves the port is open, not that the service is healthy.

-----

Settings and secrets

- Shared settings: k8s/configmaps/common.yml.
- Secrets: just k8s secrets reads .env and pipes them into kubectl apply. No file is written.
- One exception: claims-gateway-key, a mounted PEM file.

Warning
-----
A Kubernetes secret is base64, not encryption. RBAC is the real guard. For production, prefer an external manager.

-----

Hardening on every service

- allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
- Read-only root filesystem, with emptyDir at /tmp where needed
- Requests and limits set
- Liveness and readiness probes

-----

Updates

	kubectl rollout restart deployment/digital-twin -n crowdvision
	kubectl rollout status  deployment/digital-twin -n crowdvision
	kubectl rollout undo    deployment/digital-twin -n crowdvision

The old pod serves until the new one is ready.

Application images use IfNotPresent, so just k8s load works on k3d without a registry. For a real cluster see Trust & Service Mesh.

-----

Known gaps

- One replica everywhere. No autoscaler, no PodDisruptionBudget. Losing a pod is an outage.
- Databases are single instances with no backup defined here.
- :latest tags mean a rollout may not pick up new code.

-----

When something is wrong

	# why is the pod not ready? read Events at the bottom
	kubectl describe pod <pod> -n crowdvision
	# logs: current, previous crash, init container
	kubectl logs deployment/digital-twin -n crowdvision
	kubectl logs <pod> -n crowdvision --previous
	kubectl logs <pod> -n crowdvision -c wait-for-db
	# shell inside
	kubectl exec -it <pod> -n crowdvision -- sh
	# recent events
	kubectl get events -n crowdvision --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
	# which image is really running
	kubectl get pod <pod> -n crowdvision -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}'

k3d refuses connections after a restart? Find the port mapped to 6443:

	docker ps --filter name=k3d-crowdvision-serverlb
	kubectl config set-cluster k3d-crowdvision --server=https://127.0.0.1:<PORT>

entries.title: Observability
entries.content:
Observability

MetricScrapeAlert ruleTracecAdvisorWordA number measured over timePrometheus reading a service’s /metrics“Fire when this number looks bad”One request followed across servicesBuilt-in container stats on each nodeMeaningtelemetry_ingest_totalEvery few secondsServiceDownNot builtCPU per podExample

How a problem gets noticed, and what stays invisible.

-----

The short version

MetricsAlert rulesLogsTracesSignal6 of 11 backend servicesYes, but they tell nobodyEach service’s stdout, not collectedNone across services. agent alone sends LLM traces to LangfuseState

-----

Who exposes what

All six use the Rust prometheus crate.

telemetrydigital-twinnotificationchatdashboardsocketServicetelemetry_ingest_total, persist failures, publish outcomes, telemetry_http_*http_requests_total, http_error_requests_total, http_request_duration_secondsSame three nameschat_http_*telemetry_fanout_latency_ms, events in and outMessages relayed, skipped, connections refused, clients connectedMeasures

No metrics at all: agent, claims-gateway, tenancy, registry, provisioner.

HTTP metrics label the route template, never the real URL, so ids cannot explode the series.

-----

Local vs cluster settings

Each environment has its own Prometheus and Grafana: compose starts one pair locally, the cluster runs another. Only one pair runs at a time. Their settings differ:

ConfigFinds targetsReach itHistoryprometheus.yml, prometheus.rules.ymlFixed list/prometheus/, /grafana/Image defaultLocalk8s/monitoring/prometheus.ymlPods annotated prometheus.io/scrape/grafana only15 days, 5 GiCluster

The cluster also scrapes what no code exposes:

kubernetes-cadvisoristiodistio-ztunnelistio-ingress-gatewayJobCPU, memory, disk of every pod, the only signal covering all servicesControl plane health, certificatesmTLS proxy stats per nodeRequests at the edgeShows

-----

Alert rules

ServiceDownTwinServiceHighErrorRate, ChatServiceHighErrorRate, SensorServiceHighErrorRateTwinServiceHighLatency, ChatServiceHighLatency, SensorServiceHighLatencyContractsServiceFanoutLatencyHighSensorIngestPersistFailuresSensorIngestStalledSensorTelemetryFanoutFailingAlertA target stops answeringOver 5% errorsp95 over 1 sp95 fan-out over 500 msReadings fail to saveNo accepted reading in 10 minPublishing failsFires when

The queries name no job, so one rule set fits both stacks. They work because a metric name normally belongs to one service.

Trap: in the cluster digital-twin and notification share metric names, so the Twin rules really add up both services.

-----

Gaps

- Nobody gets told. No Alertmanager, so an alert only shows on Prometheus’s page.
- Rules are copied by hand between the two stacks, and have drifted: the cluster still has NodeEventLoopLagHigh, for Node services that no longer exist.
- Local misses notification: it is not in prometheus.yml.
- No alert yet on socket’s relay_messages_skipped_total or socket_connections_rejected_total, nor on notification’s dead-letter topic.
- Control plane is invisible: a failing sign-in shows nowhere.

entries.title: Frontend Architecture
entries.content:
Frontend Architecture

SPAComposableStoreTresJSTSLInstanced meshSpriteWordOne web page that redraws itselfA reusable piece of stateful Vue logicState shared across pagesVue components for three.js, the 3D librarythree.js shader language, runs on the GPUOne drawing call for many copiesA flat image that always faces the cameraMeaningThe whole appuseThemestores/domainsTresCanvasghost styleAll roomsA sensor pinExample

Package: frontend/ · Stack: Vue 3 / Vite / Tailwind CSS v4 / TresJS / vue-i18n

One app, organised by feature first, by job second: a folder per page, and inside it a folder per job.



-----

Layout

views/<feature>/components/<feature>/<role>/components/commons/composables/<feature>/utils/<feature>/types/<feature>/stores/<feature>/services/socket.tsrouter/routes.tsPathOne routed page per feature: homepage, dashboard, digital-twin, domains, administration, authenticationThat page’s parts, e.g. dashboard/{header,kpi,table,charts}, digital-twin/{scene,controls,buildings,rooms,modals}base (buttons, badges, cards), forms, overlays (modal, popover), layout (app shell, nav bar), navigation, account, chat, notifications, data (pagination, clock)Stateful logic, in the feature that owns it; shared ones (useApi, useTheme, chat, live sensor data) in commons/Pure logic, unit-tested beside the file it coversTypes only: wire shapes and component-facing types, no runtime code except enumsPinia stores: authentication, domains, digital-twin (buildings), commons (notifications, sensor data)The one Socket.IO client, shared by every featureEvery path, read by the router and the nav linksHolds

- Every layer (views, components, composables, utils, types, stores) splits by feature the same way; code used by two features with no clear owner goes in commons/.
- A feature imports commons/ freely. It imports another feature only for a part that feature owns: administration reuses domains/modals/CreateDomainModal.vue and domains/badges/RoleBadge.vue.
- Views compose; they hold no markup a child could own. Every view except the homepage loads lazily.
- Logic that needs no ref goes in utils/, so it is unit-tested (dashboard summary, pagination window, chart timeline, building grouping, floor-plan preview extent, colour bands). Components stay untested and are covered by e2e/ and backend/acceptance/.

Design System

Colours are Material 3 roles, declared once in src/assets/main.css:

- :root holds the light palette, and .dark overrides the same --cv-* variables.
- @theme inline exposes them as Tailwind colours: bg-surface-container-low, text-on-surface-variant, bg-primary, …
- Components use roles only, never a palette step like emerald-600. A new theme is therefore one CSS block.
- Sections separate by tone, spacing and shadow, not by divider lines: tables use zebra rows with rounded ends, and modals have no header or footer rules.

text-display-clock … text-label-headersurface-cardshadow-soft, shadow-liftfieldTone (utils/commons/tone.ts)TokenType scale; Inter, tabular figuresCard surface: large radius, shadow-soft, faint ring; no drawn borderResting cards; popovers, modals and hovered cardsEvery text input and selectSemantic colour a helper returns (statusTone, getRoleMeta, SEVERITY_TONE); BaseBadge and StatusDot map it to rolesUse

- The theme is light, dark or system. It is stored in localStorage['theme'], and useTheme toggles .dark on <html>.
- Chart.js and the 3D canvas cannot read CSS variables. useChartTheme resolves them to literals again after each theme change, and BuildingScene swaps its clear colour.
- Icons are Phosphor, rendered through BaseIcon, which takes the name without the ph- prefix.
- Data-viz colours stay literal: temperature and air-quality bands (utils/digital-twin/colors.ts) and QR codes, because their meaning must not change with the theme.

3D Twin Scene

- A room position is the box centre on every axis, so a storey’s floor is at y - height / 2.
- The scene draws snapRooms(rooms) (utils/digital-twin/snapRooms.ts), not the raw rooms: gaps up to SNAP_GAP (0.75: the dev building’s wall gaps reach 0.6, its corridors start at 0.9) between facing walls on one storey close to zero; wider gaps are left alone. A wall moves only when close neighbours cover all of it, so a wall that also faces a corridor never pushes into it. Two covered walls meet halfway; a covered wall facing an uncovered one moves the whole gap. A last pass caps any two facing walls at half their gap each, so snapping never adds an overlap. Horizontal only; the room data is unchanged.
- The room batch always holds every room on screen, in a fixed order (partitionRooms, utils/digital-twin/roomPartition.ts). The selected room is drawn on its own as the overlay and collapsed to zero scale inside the batch — not removed — and so is the exploded one; a zero-size instance draws nothing and cannot be hit by a raycast. batchKey, the :key of RoomInstances, ThermalGlow and AirHaze, is built from the rooms on screen and must never depend on selection: when it did, every click remounted all three and rebuilt their GPU state — counted at the WebGPU device over 7 clicks, 6 render pipelines, 12 shader modules and 48 buffers, where the whole scene loads with 2 and 12. Now a click rewrites instance matrices only.
- The glow and haze layers follow the same rule: thermalGlows and airHazes return one entry per room on screen, lit only where there is a reading, and a mode that is off passes no readings rather than an empty list. Unlit rooms collapse to zero scale, so the layers are built once per room set: switching a colour mode on used to remount its layer and compile a pipeline every time (1 pipeline and 7–8 buffers per switch, counted at the device), and now allocates nothing. AirHaze pumps frames only while some haze is lit — it now stays mounted in every mode, and an unconditional pump would render continuously.
- Materials are cached, not disposed on a switch (createMaterialCache, utils/digital-twin/materialCache.ts): disposing threw the compiled pipeline away, so every render-style or theme switch — even back to the starting one — compiled again. RoomInstances caches per mount (its material binds that batch’s edge buffers); the selected-room overlay shares one cache for the scene’s lifetime (selectedRoomMaterials), since it remounts on every selection. After the first frame the other style is compiled ahead with renderer.compileAsync on throwaway meshes — with an instance colour like the real batch (another vertex layout is another pipeline) and the real scene as third argument (lights are part of the shader; without it the probe gets an unlit variant). Measured at the device, first use of temperature, air and selection — in either style — now allocates nothing. The one compile left is the batch’s first switch to the other style: the depth style reads the drawn mesh’s own bounding sphere, so a probe cannot stand in for it, and warming the real mesh would swap its material mid-compile and risk a flicker.
- Toolbar camera moves glide instead of jumping (animateTo, composables/digital-twin/useSceneControls.ts): 400 ms, eased (easeInOut, interpolateView in utils/digital-twin/camera.ts), camera and OrbitControls target together. The scene renders on demand, so each tick asks for a frame. Reset, zoom, top view and room focus all glide; zoom starts from wherever the camera is, so a click mid-glide continues from there. Grabbing the scene fires OrbitControls @start and cancels the glide at once; reduced motion jumps. cientos exposes the controls as instance, not value — reading .value silently finds none, and the target never moves. frontend/e2e/camera.spec.ts checks the glide, the jump under reduced motion and the cancel through canvas pixels (the camera has no DOM handle).
- Rooms are one InstancedMesh and draw front faces only. Two rooms sharing a wall then draw it once from each side, with no extra overdraw.
- Every line is drawn once: hiddenEdges(drawnRooms) (snapRooms.ts) flags per room the edges another room also draws. walls (−x, +x, −z, +z): top and bottom edges, when touching neighbours of the same height cover the whole wall; of two walls covering each other, the one facing −x or −z hides. corners: the vertical edge, when another room has one in the same spot at least as tall (of equals, the first keeps it), flagged 1/2/3 as that room shares an x face, a z face, or both; rooms meeting only diagonally share no face and keep both. A partition meeting the middle of a wall keeps its vertical line.
- Hiding is view-dependent, because an edge shows only through a camera-facing face: a room drops a shared line from its top, bottom or shared face always, but from the wall between the two rooms only while the camera is past the edge’s plane, so the neighbour’s face there is lit. Base lines seen from above therefore stay. The flags are per face, so the vertex stage resolves them (varying, rounded back to 0/1 per pixel) and each pixel only measures distance. RoomInstances passes hiddenWalls and hiddenCorners as per-instance vec4s; the selected room keeps its full outline. Cost: ~+0.3–0.5 ms/frame at 3.2 MP on an Intel Xe iGPU.
- Rooms are drawn by a render style (composables/digital-twin/renderStyles/): a RenderStyle returns the material for a room or the selected room, per theme. RENDER_STYLES lists them.
- useRenderStyle holds the current style for every room mesh and saves it in localStorage['renderStyle']. parseRenderStyle falls back to ghost for a missing or retired id.
- The paint-brush button in SceneToolbar switches to the next style (nextRenderStyle, wrapping round); its tooltip names the current one (model.controls.renderStyles.<id> in i18n.ts).
- ghost (renderStyles/ghostShell.ts) is a TSL fresnel, nearly clear face-on and firmer edge-on, plus an edge glow a fixed number of screen pixels wide, so outlines stay crisp at any zoom. edgeGlow (renderStyles/nodes.ts) measures it with fwidth of the face uv, or, for the instanced unit boxes, of positionGeometry, which names each edge by the two box planes it lies on, so flagged edges drop out.
- depth (renderStyles/depthFade.ts) fades rooms by distance from the camera: faint up to the building’s centre, solid toward its far edge, with the same edge glow. The range comes from the drawn mesh’s bounding sphere (focusSphere in renderStyles/nodes.ts, refreshed per object each frame), so it holds at any zoom and building size. The selected room keeps one steady opacity.
- TSL runs only on WebGPURenderer, so BuildingScene always uses it. It falls back to WebGL2 by itself when the browser has no WebGPU.
- Dark theme blends shells additively, so they glow. Light theme blends normally, because additive colour disappears on a pale background.
- Every style’s numbers and colours live in utils/digital-twin/renderStyleConfig.ts, kept private. Read them only through renderStyleConfig(id), which is typed per style.
- Temperature colour is relative to each room’s own maxTemperature (default 27 °C): temperatureColor blends TEMPERATURE_SCALE stops set in °C below the limit (blue at −12, sky, neutral teal at −5 for comfort, a pale grey at −4 so the blend never turns green, amber, orange, red at the limit). Room list, scene and legend share it.
- In temperature mode the colour is a glow, not the shell: ThermalGlow fills each room with a reading in its temperature colour, strongest at the floor and fading to clear at the ceiling. Comfortable rooms (8–4 °C below their limit) glow at COMFORT_GLOW; drifting rooms rise to full with temperatureDeviation (utils/digital-twin/thermalGlow.ts). Shells fall back to idleColor. Rooms without a reading never glow. The glow ignores clicks.
- In air-quality mode AirHaze fills each room with a reading with drifting streaks in its aqiColor (smooth AQI_SCALE: teal up to 30, a pale grey at 42 so the blend never turns green, amber at 50, red from 100). hazeFor (utils/digital-twin/airHaze.ts) makes clean air light and quick, poor air thick and slow. The pattern is world-space noise slid by time.
- Blending runs in linear light, so a translucent colour over the near-white light background comes out pale. ThermalGlow and AirHaze pass their opacity through themeOpacity (colors.ts), which boosts it on the light theme and caps it at opaque.
- A test scene must set :tone-mapping="NoToneMapping" like BuildingScene: TresJS defaults to ACES, which greys the light background and crushes the dark one.
- The scene renders on demand, so AirHaze requests a frame on every animation tick while mounted. requestAnimationFrame stops in hidden tabs; with prefers-reduced-motion the haze stays still and requests no frames.
- The scene legend is one gradient bar per mode (temperatureGradient, aqiGradient). The dashboard, which has no per-room limit, keeps TEMPERATURE_BANDS and AQI_BANDS.
- Each style has an idleColor per theme for rooms with no reading (ghost: slate on light, pale grey on dark). Data colours (temperature, air quality) stay in colors.ts and never change with the theme.

Sensor Editor

Who owns what. Telemetry owns a sensor (id, name, device kind, room); digital-twin owns only its position. The frontend joins the two lists on sensorId (joinSensorsWithPlacements, utils/digital-twin/sensors.ts); a placement whose sensor is gone is dropped, never drawn.

- provideSensorEditor (composables/digital-twin/useSensorEditor.ts) creates one editor per twin view and shares it by provide/inject, not a store. SceneToolbar sits inside BuildingScene, so props would have to thread through the scene.
- The toolbar’s broadcast button turns edit mode on, and shows only to an editing role in the building’s domains. Every edit goes into a local draft (utils/digital-twin/sensorDraft.ts); nothing is sent until Save in SensorEditBar.
- previewSensors is the saved state with the draft applied. The editor exposes it as rows; the room list (RoomSensors), the unplaced list (UnplacedSensors) and the scene read it, so they cannot disagree.
- A draft names one building’s rooms: switching building, leaving the route, closing the tab and leaving edit mode all ask before discarding it. A draft ref is time plus random, not crypto.randomUUID, which throws on a plain-http origin other than localhost.
- Save is two batches, telemetry first because it generates the ids twin keys placements by (useSensorDraft). A twin failure after telemetry succeeded keeps the unsent placements apart from the draft (mergePlacementBatches), so a retry never creates a sensor twice and sensors added meanwhile are still sent.
- The add form offers device kinds, not metrics: useDeviceKinds reads /telemetry/devices once per session. A router is one card, though it reports two metrics. Labels are translated by kind (model.sensors.devices.<kind>) and fall back to the server’s label; icons use sensorIcon with a generic fallback, so a new kind needs no frontend change.

What the scene draws.

- Pins and room badges are sprites, not DOM. A cientos Html overlay projects itself and writes a DOM transform every frame — measured on an Intel Iris Xe at pixel ratio 2, ~0.35 ms of main thread each, so 60 sensors turned a 16.7 ms frame into 50 ms. A sprite is billboarded on the GPU: 123 sensors now cost ~6.6 ms of main thread per frame and hold 16.7 ms. The one Html element left is the tooltip of the hovered pin.
- useSpriteLayer builds the sprites imperatively under a TresGroup and keeps them in step with the list, as RoomInstances does for its mesh. The scene renders with WebGPURenderer, which only draws node materials (SpriteNodeMaterial, from three/webgpu), and Tres can handle neither kind of hand-off: as a prop it re-patches the sprite every render (“maximum recursive updates”), and as a tag it has no constructor for it. e2e/sensors-mode.spec.ts switches the mode on and fails on either.
- Textures come from useIconTextures: a disc with the device kind’s glyph, read from the Phosphor font the app already loads, or with a room’s count. One texture per icon or number and colour, one material per texture, shared by every sprite that draws it. A kind whose glyph cannot be read still gets the disc.
- Sprites made outside Tres get no Tres pointer events, so SensorSprites raycasts its own group for hover (the tooltip) and click (move, in edit mode only, never while a point is being picked).
- Both layers are mounted only in Mode.Sensors or while editing, and a kind switched off in the legend is simply left out of the list — sprites unmount cleanly, unlike Html overlays, which could leave their element behind.
- BuildingScene must not set window-size on TresCanvas: measuring the window while the canvas starts below the top bar misplaces anything projected to the screen — the hover tooltip today, every overlay before.
- The legend’s chips come from groupByType over the previewed rows — one per device kind actually present, hidden below two kinds. Every kind starts on, and a click switches that one off (hiddenTypes): a lit chip that goes grey when clicked reads the way a person expects. Adding or moving a sensor of a switched-off kind switches it back on rather than swallowing it. A room badge counts only the kinds being shown.

Devices mode. (Mode.Devices, toolbar “Show devices”)

- useDeviceDots listens for the socket devices event only while the mode is on, and holds the building’s room through the sensor store (holdRoom / releaseRoom), so leaving a metric bucket never drops the room under it.
- parseDevices refuses any other shape, including an extra key on a device: an id would follow one phone through the building. The devices.json fixture pins it.
- A tick from another building, older than the one shown, or past STALE_AFTER_MS (30 s) is dropped; a held tick past 30 s is cleared, so a stopped collector leaves no frozen dots.
- DeviceDots draws three instanced meshes: a filled dot per connected phone and a flat ring per passer-by, both 1.1 m up, and a floor halo sized to radius. dotCapacity reserves a power of two (≥ 64) and the layer remounts only when a crowd outgrows it.
- Only devices in rooms on screen (visibleDevices) are drawn, so a hidden floor shows none. Devices carry no id, so dots jump between ticks rather than glide; twin’s tracks already smooth them.

Placing a point sensor.

- GroundPlane covers the rooms on screen plus GROUND_MARGIN (20 m), sized to whole metres so its 1 m grid lands on metres, and appears only while a placement is pending. PlacementCursor raycasts the pointer against meshes named room-shell and sensor-ground — nothing else in the scene is a surface.
- snapOnSurface snaps only the axes running along the hit face, so a point on a wall stays on that wall. roomBehind reads the room just behind the face (SURFACE_DEPTH 0.05 m), so a sensor on a ceiling or an outer wall belongs to that room and one on open ground belongs to none.
- clampToGround holds every placement at or above the building’s lowest floor, clicked or typed: underground is never a real spot.
- A click picks a point rather than placing it: candidate in the editor can then be typed in PlacementHint’s x/y/z fields or moved with nudge (arrows along x/z, Shift for height), and Enter confirms. Typed coordinates lie on no surface, so the room then comes from roomAt alone.
- Moving an existing sensor reuses that flow (startMoving), so it has the same fields and keys as placing; its own pin is left out of sensorMarkers while it moves, or it would be drawn twice.
- A router given only a room (added from a room, or an unplaced one dropped on a room) gets ceilingMount: the room’s centre, CEILING_GAP (0.5 m) below its ceiling, mid-height in a room under 1 m. The position estimator needs every router’s point; exactly on the ceiling it would also touch the floor above and count there. Other kinds keep only their room badge.
- Entering edit mode drafts ceilingMountsFor every saved router with a room but no position, once sensors and placements both loaded without error — so one Save fixes routers saved before the default. A failed placements fetch drafts nothing: it would overwrite real positions.
- topView (utils/digital-twin/camera.ts) puts the camera straight above the building, high enough that the footprint plus 5 m fits the narrower of the vertical and horizontal fields of view. It moves the OrbitControls target too, so orbiting afterwards pivots on the building.

Tests. frontend/e2e/sensors.spec.ts (just test frontend-e2e) drives the real UI with telemetry and twin stubbed by Playwright routes, including a click in the canvas to place an outdoor sensor, and asserts the two batches the app sent. The services have their own suites, so stubbing them keeps the browser test about the editor.

Dashboard

- Simulator toggle (SimulatorToggle, composables/dashboard/simulator.ts): PUT / DELETE / GET /telemetry/simulation/buildings/{id}, 10 s timeout. It sends no rooms and no sensors — telemetry reads the building’s own and picks the simulators — and the browser never calls a simulator.
- Connected devices card (useConnectedDevices, utils/dashboard/connectedDevices.ts): GET /telemetry/connected-devices/buildings/{id}. Telemetry sums the rooms; the browser never adds them — a device-count report on the socket only triggers a re-read. 404 shows “No reading yet”, not 0; a report older than 5 min is flagged stale.
- A refused start (404 no simulator configured, 502 a simulator down) throws, and the toggle re-reads the status instead of trusting its optimistic flip.
- e2e/simulator.spec.ts checks the start/stop calls, that nothing reaches /simulator/, and that a refused start leaves the toggle on Start.

Shell

- App.vue mounts RouterView plus three app-wide overlays: AuthDialogs, PushNotificationPrompt and ChatWidget.
- AppLayout renders TopNavBar, and its variant sets the page body: page pads and centres it, fill gives the 3D twin the whole viewport, and bare lets the homepage lay out its own full-width sections.
- The login, sign-up and settings dialogs are one module-level state (useAuthDialog). A locked nav link, the bar and the mobile menu all open the same one.

Popovers dismiss themselves
-----
PopoverMenu closes on a pointer press outside it or on Escape (useDismiss). A popover inside a clickable card still needs @click.stop on the menu, or the card handles the click too.

entries.title: Telemetry Storage & Retention
entries.content:
Telemetry Storage & Retention

This page explains how telemetry keeps years of sensor readings without the database growing without bound. It is written to be readable without knowing Timescale — every mechanism is shown on a concrete row first.

Applies to: telemetry (Rust / Postgres + TimescaleDB). Supersedes the MongoDB time-series collections used by the Node sensor-service.

-----

The Problem, In Numbers

One building, 100 sensors, one reading every 30 seconds:

per sensor per dayper building per dayper building per year10 buildings per year2 880288 000105 million1.05 billionrows

At ~170 bytes a row that is roughly 180 GB a year, before indexes. Telemetry is written once and almost never read individually, so paying full price for every row is waste.

Three mechanisms cut it. They are independent — each helps on its own, and they multiply.

-----

Lever 1 — Store Each Fact Once

A temperature reading arrives at POST /ingest:

	{
	  "buildingId": "b1",
	  "roomId": "r1",
	  "timestamp": 1700000000000,
	  "temperature": 21.5
	}

The naive row stores all of it twice — once in typed columns, once again in the payload JSON blob:

b1building_idr1room_idtemperaturemetric2023-11-14 22:13:20+00ts21.5value{"buildingId":"b1","roomId":"r1","timestamp":1700000000000,"temperature":21.5}payload

JSON stores key names as text on every row. "buildingId" is 12 bytes, repeated 288 000 times a day, for a value that is already in the column next to it.

Rule: payload holds only what no column holds.

temperaturepeopleCountairQualitymetric4 keys4 keys12 keyspayload before{}{}8 keys — pm25, pm10, co2, voc, temperature, humidity, aqi, scenariopayload after

The stored row becomes:

b1building_idr1room_idtemperaturemetric2023-11-14 22:13:20+00ts21.5value{}payload

Nothing is lost. building_id, room_id and ts are the columns; value is the measurement the plugin designated. GET /{metric}/latest reassembles the original envelope from the columns before answering.

The list is not hand-maintained: MetricDescriptor.fields names every field a metric declares, and the plugin names the one that became value. Everything else is what gets kept.

The trim affects storage only, not the wire
-----
The Redis telemetry:raw event still carries the full payload. This changes what is written to disk, not what is published — dashboard and the browser see no difference.

-----

Lever 2 — Squeeze Rows That Repeat Each Other

Room r1 writes 2 880 rows a day. Look at what they have in common:

	b1 | r1 | temperature | 22:13:20 | 21.5 | {}
	b1 | r1 | temperature | 22:13:50 | 21.6 | {}
	b1 | r1 | temperature | 22:14:20 | 21.6 | {}
	...2877 more, all starting the same way

b1, r1 and temperature are identical on every line. The timestamps rise by exactly 30 000 ms. The values barely move.

Timescale can rewrite a batch of up to 1 000 such rows into one compressed row:

	alter table readings set (
	  timescaledb.compress,
	  timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'building_id, room_id, metric',
	  timescaledb.compress_orderby   = 'ts desc'
	);
	select add_compression_policy('readings', interval '7 days');

- compress_segmentby — these columns are stored once per batch instead of 1 000 times.
- compress_orderby — timestamps are stored as first-value-plus-differences (+30s, +30s, …) rather than 1 000 full timestamps.
- Floating-point values are stored as differences between neighbours, which are tiny when a room’s temperature drifts slowly.

Typical result on telemetry: 10–20× smaller.

Only data older than 7 days is compressed. Recent data stays in ordinary row form, so ingest stays fast and GET /{metric}/latest is unaffected. Compression runs in the background as chunks age past the threshold.

-----

Lever 3 — Keep Summaries, Not Every Reading

Nobody asks what a room measured at 03:41:30 last November. They ask for a chart.

After 14 days, individual readings are deleted and replaced by one row per hour:

	create materialized view readings_hourly
	with (timescaledb.continuous) as
	select time_bucket('1 hour', ts) as bucket,
	       building_id, room_id, metric,
	       avg(value) as avg, min(value) as min, max(value) as max,
	       sum(value) as sum, count(*) as samples
	from readings
	group by 1, 2, 3, 4;

120 raw readings per hour collapse to a single row carrying average, minimum, maximum, sum and sample count. That is 120× fewer rows, kept indefinitely.

readings itself is dropped after 14 days:

	select add_retention_policy('readings', interval '14 days');

The view refreshes incrementally on a schedule and tolerates late-arriving readings within a 3-day window, so a sensor that reconnects after an outage still lands in the right bucket.

Which table a query reads

Decided entirely by the requested time range, in the adapter:

1D1W1Mcustomrange1 hour1 day1 day1 daybucket sizereadingsreadings_hourlyreadings_hourlyreadings_hourlysource

TimeRange::bucket_interval() in the kernel already returns "1 hour" for 1D and "1 day" otherwise, so the routing is one branch in the persistence adapter. No kernel code knows either table exists.

min, max and sum combine exactly across hours. avg does not: an average of hourly averages weighs a sensor offline for 40 minutes like a full hour. The adapter reads avg as sum(sum) / sum(samples), which is the true average.

A retried batch is stored once

- readings_key is unique on (building_id, metric, room_id, ts); the insert is on conflict do nothing.
- A device that retries a batch after a timeout changes nothing: the first copy of each reading wins.
- Migration 0007 deletes duplicates stored before the key existed, compressed chunks included.
- Rollup hours materialized from duplicates more than 3 days ago keep their doubled sum; the policy never revisits them. Do not fix them with an unbounded refresh_continuous_aggregate: a window whose raw rows retention already dropped is materialized empty, erasing the history.

-----

Combined Effect

10 buildings, 100 sensors each, one reading every 30 seconds:

nothing appliedlever 1 — no duplicated payload+ lever 2 — compression after 7 days+ lever 3 — 14-day raw, hourly rollup~180 GB~110 GB~8 GB~2 GBone year of data

Estimates, not measurements. payload width dominates and depends on the real airQuality mix. Verify with:

	select pg_size_pretty(hypertable_size('readings'));
	select * from hypertable_compression_stats('readings');

A compression ratio below ~8× means payload is carrying more than it should.

-----

Compared With MongoDB Time-Series

The Node sensor-service used Mongo time-series collections. The underlying idea is the same — batch measurements, store repeated identifiers once, delta-encode time — so this is not a change of strategy, but the details differ.

batching unitidentifiers stored oncewhen it compressesrecent datarollupsbucket: same metaField, 1 h span, ≤1 000 measurementsmetaField only — was buildingon bucket close, alwaysalready compressednot built inMongo time-seriescompressed row: ≤1 000 rows per segmentevery segmentby column — building_id, room_id, metricafter 7 days, by policyplain rows, fully mutablecontinuous aggregateTimescale

Three practical differences:

- roomId was not part of metaField. Only building was. Every measurement therefore carried its own copy of the room name. Under segmentby it is stored once per batch.
- Buckets were keyed on the wrong clock. timeField was createdAt (ingest time) while every query filtered and sorted on timestamp (sensor event time), so Mongo could not skip buckets by time. Postgres has one ts column serving as both the partition key and the query key, so chunk exclusion works.
- No rollup equivalent. Mongo deleted everything at 90 days via expireAfterSeconds. Here data older than 14 days survives as hourly summaries, indefinitely.

Where Mongo was better: compression was immediate and unconditional, and typed schema fields meant no JSON key repetition — which is precisely the gap lever 1 closes.

-----

Where This Lives

tables, hypertable, compression, retentionhourly rollupunique reading keypayload trim on write, envelope re-inflation on readbucket size per rangeconcernbackend/telemetry/migrations/0002_timescale.up.sqlbackend/telemetry/migrations/0003_rollup.up.sqlbackend/telemetry/migrations/0007_readings_key.up.sqlbackend/telemetry/src/adapters/driven/postgres/readings.rsbackend/telemetry/src/types/query.rsfile

See also Communication & Data Flow.
