entries.title: Sensor Actions & the Device ACL
entries.content:
Sensor Actions & the Device ACL

Telemetry flows in: sensors push readings, the service stores and republishes them. Actions are the one path that flows out — the user turns the boiler up, and telemetry has to speak to a physical device.

Devices do not agree on anything: field names, verbs, protocols, or even which operations exist. This page describes the three-layer split that keeps that disagreement out of the domain model.

Applies to: telemetry — POST /executeAction.

-----

The Problem

The Node sensor-service had no domain model for actions at all. actions.json mapped an arbitrary string to a URL:

	{ "increase": { "123": { "url": "http://gateway/simulator/tp/control/receive",
	                         "method": "POST", "arguments": { "0": "value" } } } }

- actionName was free text typed in the UI. Nothing declared which actions exist.
- Arguments were positional — ["21"] — with no types and no validation.
- The table was keyed by individual sensorId. 500 boilers meant 500 near-identical entries.
- url and method were visible to the request handler, so HTTP was baked into the flow.

Compare with the read path, in the same service: metrics declare their fields in MetricDescriptor, get validated by check_fields, and are advertised through GET /contracts. The write path had none of it.

-----

Three Layers

Catalog — ActionSpecCommandBindingLayerper metricper requestper device driverScopewhich actions can exist, and their parameter typesthe actual instructionhow to say one action to one device familyDeclaresneveryes — this is what the ACL rewritesis the translationTranslated?

The distinction that matters: the catalog is a static declaration and is never translated. The Command is the runtime message, and it is the only thing that crosses the anti-corruption boundary.

Layer 1 — the catalog

Declared by the plugin, next to the metric’s fields, reusing the same FieldSpec type:

	static ACTIONS: &[ActionSpec] = &[
	    ActionSpec { name: "setTarget", label: "Set target temperature",
	                 parameters: &[FieldSpec { name: "target", kind: Finite, required: true }] },
	    ActionSpec { name: "increase", label: "Increase temperature",
	                 parameters: &[FieldSpec { name: "step", kind: Finite, required: false }] },
	    ActionSpec { name: "decrease", label: "Decrease temperature",
	                 parameters: &[FieldSpec { name: "step", kind: Finite, required: false }] },
	];

Absolute (setTarget) and relative (increase/decrease) are separate first-class actions, not variants of one another. A device offering only +/- buttons is not a degraded setTarget — it is a device that implements two of the three.

SensorPlugin::actions() defaults to &[], so a metric with no actuator (peopleCount, airQuality) declares nothing and needs no code.

Layer 2 — the command

	pub struct Command {
	    pub metric: String,       // "temperature"
	    pub building_id: String,
	    pub room_id: String,
	    pub sensor_id: String,
	    pub action: String,       // "setTarget"
	    pub arguments: Map<String, Value>,   // { "target": 21 }
	}

Arguments are named, matching the catalog’s parameter names. The kernel validates them with check_fields — the same function POST /ingest uses for readings. One validator, both directions.

Layer 3 — the binding (the ACL)

Keyed by driver, not by sensor:

	{
	  "tp-simulator": {
	    "setTarget": { "path": "/control/receive", "method": "POST", "fields": { "target": "value" } },
	    "increase":  { "path": "/control/step",    "method": "POST", "fields": { "step": "delta" } }
	  },
	  "acme-basic": {
	    "increase": { "path": "/dev/up",   "method": "POST", "fields": {} },
	    "decrease": { "path": "/dev/down", "method": "POST", "fields": {} }
	  }
	}

A driver is a device model, not a customer. Two businesses running the same boiler share acme-basic; five hundred identical units share one binding entry.

The binding holds the path, never the host — a device model is deployed at a different address in every building. The URL is composed, not templated:

	sensors.endpoint  +  binding.path   →   http://b-gw.local/control/receive

Two columns on sensors carry the per-unit facts:

driverendpointColumnwhich dialect this unit speakswhere this unit is reachableAnswers

acme-basic shows the +/- only case: it lists no setTarget, and its actions carry no fields. Empty parameters and empty fields are the ordinary path — check_fields(&[], {}) yields no errors and the request body is {}. No special case anywhere.

-----

Capability Is Per Sensor, Not Per Metric

GET /contracts is per metric. It can say “temperature sensors can, in principle, do these three things”. It cannot say “sensor 123 supports setTarget, sensor 456 only does +/-”.

What a specific sensor can do is the intersection:

	plugin.actions()  ∩  bindings[sensor.driver].keys()

served on the sensor listing (GET /sensors/buildings/{b}/rooms/{r}). The UI renders a slider when setTarget is present, +/- buttons when it is not, and no controls at all when the list is empty.

-----

A Command’s Journey

User sets sensor 123 in building b1 to 21 °C. The device is found by building and sensor id; the room plays no part, so an outdoor sensor or one that just moved is reached the same way.



Step by step:

1. Browser posts named arguments — { "target": 21 } — because GET /contracts told it the parameter is called target.
2. Edge strips any client-supplied x-gateway-claims, verifies the JWT once, re-injects verified claims.
3. HTTP adapter resolves the building’s domains and calls authz::can_edit_domains. Actions are edit: a standard_customer who can watch the chart cannot move the boiler.
4. Kernel resolves the plugin, finds the ActionSpec, validates the arguments. Never sees a URL.
5. ACL resolves sensor → driver → binding, renames target to value, checks the URL scheme, sends it.
6. Device replies. Non-2xx and unreachable both become 502; so does no answer within 5 s.

Error mapping

unknown metricmetric does not declare that actionmissing or wrong-typed parameterno binding for this sensornon-http(s) URL in the bindingdevice returned non-2xxdevice unreachableConditionkernelkernelkernelACLACLACLACLWhere404404400404500, message deliberately vague502502Response

The device’s own status is never forwarded verbatim — its 503 becomes our 502, because the failure is ours-talking-to-them, not the caller’s request.

200 accepted means delivered, not applied
-----
The response confirms the command reached the device, not that the room is 21 °C. Confirmation arrives seconds later through the ordinary read path: the boiler heats, the sensor reports 21.4, POST /ingest stores it, telemetry:raw reaches the browser, the chart moves. If the new value breaches maxTemp, the same ingest fires a record onto the alerts topic and the user is notified about the change they just made — no action-specific plumbing.

-----

Adding a Device Family

Two cases hide behind “this business’s sensors communicate differently”, and they land in different places.

Tier 1 — same protocol, different vocabulary

The device speaks HTTP but names the field setpoint_c and exposes a different path. Config only, no code:

	"acme-basic": {
	  "setTarget": { "path": "/thermo/set", "method": "PUT", "fields": { "target": "setpoint_c" } }
	}

New device model, new key. Nothing recompiles.

Tier 2 — different protocol

MQTT, Modbus, CoAP, or HTTP behind an auth scheme the device dictates. This needs code, but only inside the dispatch adapter:

	src/adapters/driven/dispatch/
	  mod.rs        Dispatcher — sensor → driver → binding, selects transport
	  bindings.rs   catalog loading
	  http.rs       impl Transport for Http
	  mqtt.rs       impl Transport for Mqtt      ← the new device family adds this

The binding names its transport:

	"acme-mqtt": {
	  "transport": "mqtt",
	  "increase": { "topic": "dev/42/cmd", "fields": { "step": "delta" } }
	}

ActionDispatch still has one method. Transport is internal to the adapter. For both tiers the kernel, the plugins, contracts/ and every kernel test are untouched — that is what the boundary buys.

Where the catalog lives

todaywhen a tenant needs a model we do not shipStagebindings.json embedded in the imageaction_bindings tableStoragea PR and a deployan insertAdding a model means

	create table action_bindings (
	  driver    text not null,
	  action    text not null,
	  transport text not null default 'http',
	  path      text not null,
	  method    text not null default 'POST',
	  fields    jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
	  primary key (driver, action)
	);

Note what is not in that table: a tenant, a domain, or a building. It is a global device catalog. Per-business behaviour comes entirely from which driver and endpoint a business’s sensors rows carry — the same mechanism whether a tenant has one device family or five.

The file comes first deliberately. Tier 2 needs a deploy regardless, and tier 1 changes are rare enough that a PR is the right amount of ceremony.

A tenant-editable endpoint is an SSRF primitive
-----
/executeAction makes telemetry fetch a URL with its own network identity. While the catalog is ops-owned, the http(s) scheme check is sufficient. The moment a binding or sensors.endpoint becomes editable through the API, a tenant can aim it at http://169.254.169.254/ or any internal service and read the response path’s behaviour. That case needs a host allowlist per domain, not a scheme check. Keep the catalog ops-owned until there is a concrete reason not to.

These are egress calls into a customer’s network. Under Istio ambient each reachable host needs a ServiceEntry — pair that list with the allowlist above, since it is the same list. See Trust & Service Mesh.

-----

Deliberate Omissions

- No emulating setTarget on a +/- device. Reading the current value, computing a delta and firing N increase calls is a control loop: it needs current state, is not atomic, overshoots when the sensor lags, and two concurrent requests fight each other. Control loops belong in the device or a dedicated controller, never in a translation layer. A device without an absolute setpoint honestly reports that it has none.
- No URL templating or per-sensor overrides. One binding per device family covers every sensor of that family. Add when a second family disagrees.
- No sensor-existence check in execute. “Do we know how to talk to sensor 123” is the ACL’s question, answered by DispatchError::Unconfigured → 404. A second lookup against the sensors table would answer the same question twice.
- No queued or asynchronous actions. Fire, wait, report.

-----

Where This Lives

ActionSpec, check_fieldsCommandper-metric action catalogvalidation and error mappingport — one method, protocol-freedriver lookup, field renaming, transportConcernsrc/types/plugin.rssrc/types/sensor.rssrc/plugins/temperature.rssrc/kernel/actions.rssrc/kernel/ports.rs (ActionDispatch)src/adapters/driven/dispatch.rsFile

The kernel imports nothing that names a URL, a method, or a protocol. That is the anti-corruption boundary, and tests/architecture.rs keeps it that way.

entries.title: Floor Plans as Building Models
entries.content:
Floor Plans as Building Models

Building registration accepts a JSON description of rooms, or architectural drawings in SVG, DXF or vector PDF, one per storey. This page records the decisions behind the drawings: what is extracted, what a drawing cannot supply, and where the extraction runs.

For the registration flow this feeds, see Digital Twin architecture. For the bounded context, Building Management.

-----

The Seam

The format decision lives in one place — frontend/src/components/administration/registration/RegisterBuildingModal.vue:

	loadFromJson(JSON.parse(await file.text()))

Everything downstream of loadFromJson is already format-agnostic: the draft, the per-room editor cards, the threshold sliders, the sensor drafts, and submit() posting to /twin/register. A floor plan becomes a second way to produce the same BuildingDraft.

SourcePicker — one tile per format; JSON or planscalibration and per-storey upload rowsextraction — drawing to BuildingDraftuseBuildingDraft, room cards, threshold and sensor UIPOST /twin/register, service::provisioning, the Kafka handshakeschemas/twin-schema, domain/building.rsLayeryes, one tileyes, newyes, newnononoChanges?

The backend does not learn that floor plans exist. That is the point: a drawing is an authoring convenience, and the twin’s contract is the room list either way.

The target is easier than it looks

domain/building.rs models a room as an axis-aligned box — Coordinates { x, y, z } and Dimensions { width, height, depth }. There are no polygons, no wall thicknesses, no door graph. Extraction has to produce a bounding rectangle and a label, not reconstruct the architecture.

Y is up, so the plan lies in X–Z

useInstancedRooms.ts passes position and dimensions straight into a Three.js instance matrix as translation and scale. Two consequences the JSON schema does not state:

- y is the vertical axis. A drawing’s two axes are x and z, and height is the ceiling. Mapping a plan’s vertical axis to y mirrors the storey into the floor.
- position is the box centre, on every axis — a BoxGeometry is origin-centred. A rectangle’s top-left corner is not a position; the centre is.

Reading the plan from above makes the sense of the axes agree without a flip: SVG’s downward y is the same direction as +z on screen when looking down the y axis.

The draft editor is the accuracy backstop

Extraction is never trusted. Its output lands in the same reviewable draft a hand-written JSON does, and the user corrects it before anything is submitted. The bar is “close enough to fix in half a minute”, not correctness. Work that chases extraction accuracy instead of improving the editor is solving the wrong problem.

-----

What a Drawing Cannot Tell You

Four of the six room fields are absent from any plan view, and the missing ones are not guessable from the geometry.

x, z, width, depthyheightcapacitycolorFieldyesnonever — a plan is a horizontal sectionneversometimes — a fillOn the plan?extracted, after calibrationfloor_index × floor_height; one drawing is one floordefault, editable per roomleft unset; the editor’s own default, as for hand-written JSONleft unset; the editor’s own defaultWhere it comes from

Only geometry is extracted. capacity and color are the two fields a drawing has no authority over, and loadFromJson already defaults both for every other upload — so extraction leaves them alone rather than inventing a second set of defaults that has to be kept in step.

Deriving capacity from floor area was considered and dropped. Occupancy per square metre is a function of room use, which a plan does not encode, so the number would be wrong at a plausible-looking magnitude — worse than the blank the user already expects to fill in.

-----

Scale Is a Calibration, Not a Heuristic

The twin declares no unit. A drawing carries pixels, or drawing units, or a printed scale bar — nothing that resolves itself. There are exactly two honest sources:

- Declared by the format. DXF states $INSUNITS. Take it.
- Declared by the user. They type how many drawing units make a metre, then check a room’s width in the editor and adjust. Re-extraction is instant and non-destructive, so the loop is the calibration.

There is no third option. Inferring metres from a bitmap’s dimensions, a door’s typical width, or a text label that happens to read 1:100 is guessing dressed as convenience, and it fails silently — a building that is uniformly 3× too large still renders, still registers, and is only noticed once someone stands in it.

When the format declares a scale the calibration control is pre-filled, not hidden. Drawings lie about their units often enough that the knob has to stay reachable.

A two-point measuring tool over a preview of the drawing is the friendlier control and was deliberately not built: it needs a rendered, click-mapped preview, which is more work than the rest of the upload path combined. The number field is the same calibration with a worse first guess, and the editor already shows whether the guess was right. Build the picker when a real drawing proves the number is unusable.

-----

Room Ids Must Be Deterministic

Telemetry keys per-room thresholds by path — /telemetry/thresholds/peopleCount/buildings/{buildingId}/rooms/{roomId}. An id that changes between two extractions of the same drawing orphans every threshold attached to the old one.

- Prefix every id with its storey — f0-, f1-. Two floors of an office both hold an Office 1, and a shared collision suffix would decide the winner by upload order and renumber the survivors whenever a floor is removed.
- Derive the rest from the room label when the drawing has one, slugified.
- With no label, derive it from the room’s position in drawing coordinates — stable under re-export, unlike an array index, which reorders whenever the drawing tool reorders its entity list.
- Collisions get a suffix. Two rooms named Office are normal; two rooms with the same id are a data-loss bug.

Determinism pays a second time inside the modal. Changing the scale re-extracts every drawing, and because ids come from the storey and the label rather than array order, sensors already attached to a room stay attached across the re-run. Calibration is therefore free to be a loop instead of a decision made before upload.

-----

What Counts as a Room

A drawing is mostly not rooms. Walls, furniture, dimension lines, north arrows, the sheet border and the title block all sit in the same file, and none of them are spaces. One rule separates them:

A shape is a room when a text label falls inside it.

- A label belongs to the tightest shape enclosing it, so a room’s name is not captured by the sheet it is drawn on.
- A shape enclosing another room is a container — the sheet border, the building outline — and is dropped even when a title block gave it a label of its own. Only labelled shapes count as the thing enclosed: a plan draws desks and fixtures inside rooms, and treating those as enclosed rooms would delete every room that contains one.
- Everything unlabelled is dropped silently. Walls are the common case, and a warning per wall is noise that trains the user to ignore warnings.

The ceiling is stated plainly: an unlabelled room is not extracted. Rooms are named on plans nearly always, and the alternative — treating every closed shape as a space — produces a draft in which the real rooms are buried among furniture. Adding a room by hand costs less than finding twelve wrong ones.

-----

Formats

Each format is one extractor plus an arm in the type switch; the contract below keeps it that way. The three cover what building-drawing tools export.

SVG — firstDXF — secondPDF, vector — thirdFormatDOMParser; rect, polygon, polyline and straight-line path extents, enclosed text as the labelASCII group-code pairs; LWPOLYLINE extents, TEXT/MTEXT labelspdf.js down to path bounding boxes, then identical to SVGMechanismnone — the browser already parses itnone — hand-rolled, see belowpdfjs-dist, dynamically importedNew dependencyuser$INSUNITS, user-overridableuserScale from

An architect usually hands over DXF, rarely SVG. SVG is supported because the browser parses it for free. Calibration, floor handling, id minting and the editor round trip are shared by all three readers.

-----

The Extraction Contract

One pure function per format, and it reads geometry only:

	(bytes: ArrayBuffer) => PlanReading | Promise<PlanReading>   // { shapes, warnings }

Bytes rather than text, because a PDF is binary: File.text() replaces every invalid UTF-8 sequence before a reader could see it, which silently corrupts the content stream. The two text formats decode in the dispatch table, so svg.ts and dxf.ts never learn the distinction. A reader may be async for the same reason — pdf.js is loaded on demand.

Turning shapes into rooms is a second, format-agnostic step:

	(floors: PlanFloor[], options: PlanOptions) => ExtractedBuilding

The split is what makes a multi-storey building possible. Scale, centring, elevation and id minting need to see every storey at once, so they cannot live inside a per-file reader. building is exactly the JSON loadFromJson already consumes, so no draft-building logic is duplicated.

Reading the File is the caller’s job, not the extractor’s: the seam already awaits file.text() for the JSON path, and a function over a string is the one that tests without a DOM fixture harness.

warnings is the honest channel for what a drawing contains and the schema cannot hold — a rotated room, a curved outline. Reporting them beats silently squaring them off.

Three rules, and they are the whole insurance policy:

- No Vue, no store, no network. An extractor reads bytes and returns data.
- Fixtures are the contract. Real drawings in, expected BuildingDraft JSON out, asserted per format.
- Dispatch is a switch on file type, not a plugin registry. Adding a format adds a file and an arm.

Held to those, moving one format to a service later is a swapped call site with the fixtures reused as-is — not a migration.

-----

Three formats, three coordinate conventions

SVG’s y grows downwards; DXF’s and PDF’s grow upwards; the twin’s z runs down the screen. Each reader negates y at its own boundary, so draft.ts sees one convention and normalises against it. A missed flip mirrors the whole floor — and a mirrored building still renders, still registers and still looks plausible, so nothing downstream catches it. Both flipping readers assert it in a test for that reason.

Reviewing before submitting

The draft editor lists rooms as cards, which is the right shape for correcting a name or a capacity and the wrong one for noticing that a room landed in the wrong place. The preview draws the extracted building from above, one plan per storey, in metres — the same view the user uploaded, so a misread wall or a bad scale is visible at a glance rather than inferable from a column of numbers.

It is read-only on purpose. Editing stays in the cards; the preview exists to make an error obvious, not to fix it.

-----

Where Extraction Runs

In the frontend, beside loadFromJson. No new service, no route, no image, no auth surface, no services.json entry.

The instinct to put it behind an API is usually about accuracy, and that instinct is wrong here: SVG, DXF and vector PDF parse to the same bounding boxes on either side of the wire. There is no precision to be gained by moving, and a service would cost a services.json entry, an image, a route and an auth surface for work that runs once per building.

The drawing also never leaves the browser, which is worth keeping: a floor plan is a description of a customer’s premises.

-----

Deliberate Omissions

- No polygon rooms. The twin models axis-aligned boxes. Extracting an L-shaped room’s true outline produces geometry nothing downstream can store or render. Its bounding box is the honest answer; splitting it into two rooms is the user’s call, in the editor.
- The source drawing is not stored. The twin persists the derived room list. Retaining the original is document management — retention windows, per-tenant storage, access control — and none of it serves occupancy.
- One drawing is one floor. A site plan holding three buildings, or a sheet holding four floors, is split by the user before upload. Detecting the split is inference on top of inference. Several drawings do make one building: the upload takes a row per storey, placed against one shared origin.
- Storeys are aligned by the drawings, not by the extractor. One origin is taken across every floor, so a wing that genuinely sits east of the one below stays east of it. The cost is the mirror case: two exports of the same footprint with different sheet margins land displaced by exactly that difference, and nothing detects it. Aligning them instead would mean assuming every storey’s top-left corner is the same point, which is false for any building that changes shape as it rises. The drawings have to agree on a coordinate space; the extractor cannot invent one.
- No rotated or skewed rooms. The schema stores axis-aligned boxes. A rotate or matrix transform has no correct box, so the shape is skipped and counted in warnings rather than squared off into a plausible wrong rectangle.
- No curved outlines. A path carrying a curve command is not a room outline — it is a door swing or a logo — and is left alone.
- Only translate and scale transforms are honoured. They cover CAD and Inkscape exports. Ignoring transforms entirely would silently displace every room on a layered drawing.
- No DXF parser library. The subset a room outline needs — group-code pairs, LWPOLYLINE extents, TEXT/MTEXT — is about a hundred lines. A library would also read BLOCKS, which is the one thing worth having, but its coverage cannot be judged without real drawings, and a new npm dependency means regenerating the Linux lockfile. Revisit when a real export proves blocks are common.
- No rooms inside blocks. A DXF that draws its rooms in BLOCKS and places them with INSERT yields nothing. The reader counts the INSERTs and says so, rather than returning an empty building that looks like a bad drawing.
- No PDF written by hand. SVG and DXF are text formats worth hand-rolling; a PDF content stream is compressed binary and is not. pdfjs-dist is the one dependency the readers add, loaded through a dynamic import so its 1.3 MB worker is a separate chunk rather than part of the main bundle — most sessions never open a PDF.
- The pdf.js legacy build, not the modern one. The modern build calls Uint8Array.prototype.toHex, which is too new for the test runtime and for browsers this app still supports.
- Only page 1 of a PDF. One drawing is one floor. A multi-page PDF is read as its first page and says so in warnings, rather than silently merging storeys.
- No plugin architecture for formats. Four formats is a switch statement.
- No capacity or colour extraction at all. Both have editor defaults that apply to every upload; a second set of defaults inside the extractor is drift waiting to happen.

-----

Testing

Each reader, drawing in, rooms outModal: file picked, scale changed, rooms shownUpload, review, submit, building in the sceneWhatFixtures in __fixtures__/, one *.spec.ts per formatBy handNothingCovered by

Why no automated end-to-end test:

- backend/acceptance is Python over HTTP and stubs the twin (stubs/twin.conf). It cannot run a TypeScript extractor.
- frontend/e2e runs Playwright with the services stubbed (sensors.spec.ts). It has no login flow, no composed stack in CI and no canvas assertions.
- Building that harness is a decision for the whole frontend, not for one modal.

-----

Where This Lives

All paths are under frontend/src/.

format dispatch, and merging storeys into one buildingshapes to rooms — scale, centring, elevation, idsSVG reader — transforms, extents, label matchingDXF reader — group-code pairs, $INSUNITS, y-axis flipPDF reader — pdf.js path bounds, y-axis flipfixtures and assertionsdraft shape, unchangedthe seam — format choice, calibration, warningsone upload row per storeyreview before submitting — one plan view per floorConcernutils/administration/floorplan/index.tsutils/administration/floorplan/draft.tsutils/administration/floorplan/svg.tsutils/administration/floorplan/dxf.tsutils/administration/floorplan/pdf.tsutils/administration/floorplan/{svg,dxf,pdf,index}.spec.ts, __fixtures__/composables/administration/useBuildingDraft.tscomponents/administration/registration/{RegisterBuildingModal,PlanCalibration}.vuecomponents/administration/registration/PlanUploadModal.vuecomponents/administration/registration/BuildingPreviewModal.vue, geometry in utils/administration/floorplan/preview.tsFile

draft.ts names no format and svg.ts names no Vue symbol. So a new format is one reader beside svg.ts and touches nothing else.

Extraction lives under utils/, not composables/, because none of it touches ref, computed or a lifecycle hook — the use prefix promises a setup()-only call site, and these are pure functions callable from anywhere.

Nothing under backend/ appears in this table, and that is the invariant worth keeping: a floor plan is an authoring format, and the twin’s contract is the room list.

Y is up, so the plan lies in X–Z
The draft editor is the accuracy backstop
What a Drawing Cannot Tell You
Scale Is a Calibration, Not a Heuristic

entries.title: Wireless People Flow
entries.content:
Wireless People Flow

Where people are in a building, live, from the Wi-Fi signals their phones already emit: a dot per phone on the twin, and room counts stored as metrics.

Status: phase 1 built on simulated routers; not yet tried on a real OpenWrt site. Tracks issue #314.

Applies to: devices/ap-collector, telemetry (/telemetry/observations, three router metrics), digital-twin (the estimator), socket (the devices event). No new service.

Two phases, in order
-----
Phase 1 — routers only. Poll the access points the building already has, and listen to the probe requests they hear. Zero new hardware.

Phase 2 — dedicated sniffers. Raspberry Pi rigs in monitor mode, for devices the routers miss. Only after phase 1 is proven in a real building.

-----

What Crosses Into CrowdVision

The Dutch DPA is explicit: “Storing multiple location points per device means that the data is not anonymous.” So the design keeps a phone’s identity on site and never stores a position.

MAC addressToken (random, secrets.token_hex(8), never derived from the MAC)PositionRoom countsDatacollector memory onlysigned tick, Kafka wifi-observations, twin memorytwin memory (one per track, no history), Redis pub/sub twin:devices:{id}Timescale readingsWhere it existswhile the phone is heard10 min on Kafka; in twin, until unseen for 3 ticksthe current tick onlythe platform’s retention (below)How long

Invariants:

- No MAC leaves the site. The collector swaps every address for a minted token; nothing turns a token back.
- No position is stored. Twin keeps each track’s current position only. Dots go out on Redis pub/sub, nowhere else.
- A dot carries no id. twin_schema::Device refuses unknown fields, so socket drops a dot carrying a token.
- Only counts are stored: totalDeviceCount, ratioDeviceCount, estimatedOccupancy.

This is pseudonymous personal data while it is live
-----
A token follows one phone for as long as it stays, and Kafka holds ten minutes of them. A dot has no id, but a viewer watching a near-empty building can follow one dot from tick to tick. So a site needs a legal basis and a notice before enabling it (Wi-Fi terms, employment agreement), exactly as for any Wi-Fi analytics. Turning off probes (subscribeProbes: false) limits it to people who joined the Wi-Fi.

-----

What Is Stored, And Why That Is Safe

A count carries no identifier and no per-device row, so there is nothing to single out. That is the whole argument for the stored data, and it is only as strong as the two conditions below.

Why Routers-Only Works

The obvious objection: MAC addresses are randomized, so won’t one phone look like a different person to every access point it passes?

No — randomization is per-SSID, not per-AP. Every AP in the building broadcasts the same SSID, so a device roaming across them keeps one address.

Android 10–15Apple (iOS 18 / macOS Sequoia)PlatformPersistent randomized MAC derived from the network profile (SSID + security type). Stable across APs, stable across forget-and-rejoin, until factory reset.On WPA2-AES or WPA3, the private address is fixed per SSID. Only open and pre-WPA2 networks rotate — every 2 weeks.Behaviour on the building SSID

Wi-Fi roaming requires this. The DHCP lease, L2 forwarding tables and 802.11r fast transition are all keyed on the station MAC. If it changed on roam, open TCP connections would drop and roaming would not function.

The objection is correct for the other regime
-----
Probe-request MACs are random per scan burst and uncorrelated between listeners. So a probe address is never counted: the collector groups one address’s frames into a burst (one scan), gives the burst a fresh token, and the twin only places it.

Two regimes

Associated — device joined the Wi-FiUnassociated — visitor never joinsRegimeEvery frame, continuously, stable per-SSID MAC, RSSI per APSporadic probe requests, streamed by hostapd (subscribeProbes, off by default)What the AP seesYes. This is phase 1.Partly. Bursts place passing dots; counting them is phase 2.Routers-only?

Phase 1 covers everyone on the Wi-Fi and misses the walk-through visitor. For facility management the associated population is generally the population that matters.

It is also the only regime with a workable legal basis: a captive portal, Wi-Fi terms of service or an employment agreement supports consent or legitimate interest. Ambient sniffing of passers-by supports neither — that is what the AP fined a Dutch municipality for in 2021. That is why subscribeProbes is off by default: a site turns it on only with a basis for it.

-----

Positions, Estimated in the Twin

Digital-twin owns the floor plan and the router placements, so it places the phones. Telemetry never sees a coordinate, and no copy of the geometry can go stale when a router moves.

How a phone is placed (service/estimator.rs, service/tracks.rs):

- Each floor is cut into 0.5 m cells inside rooms. Each cell stores the signal every router on the floor should hear from it: −40 dBm at 1 m, path-loss exponent 2.2, 5 dB per wall.
- A connected phone’s track is a posterior over cells: each tick weighs every cell by how well it explains the phone’s signals, and by distance from the last position (spread grows 0.5 m/s; cells beyond 2 m/s of walking are cut). A token unseen for 3 ticks is dropped.
- A burst (one scan heard by several routers) gets a fix: the cell whose expected signals fit best. It joins a track only when exactly one connected phone explains it within 9 dB. A burst fitting none is a passing dot (connected: false); one fitting two is dropped.

Why a grid fit, not circles. Fitting circles (trilateration) needs every distance right, but walls and weak antennas only ever lower a signal, so every circle comes out too big. Measured on 470 simulated bursts: right room 95% for the grid fit, 69% for circles.

Measured on a recorded run (tests/data/wifi-recording.jsonl, 15 min, 48 phones, simulated):

Right roomRoom counts, total offPosition error79.4%1 462median 4.0 m, p90 8.1 mDots75.0%1 988—Each phone in its router’s room

- Nearly all of it comes from memory between ticks, not from bursts: linking by place almost never fires, since most bursts fit two phones on one router.
- The simulator’s radio and scan rates are guesses; a real walk test decides the real numbers.

Fine Timing Measurement (802.11mc/az/bk) stays rejected: it is client-initiated, so the infrastructure never learns the position unless an app reports it back.

-----

Phase 1 — Routers-Only



The collector

A small daemon on the building network. Polls each AP every pollIntervalS (10 s), holds one in-memory token table, posts one signed Wi-Fi tick per building per poll to /telemetry/observations (schemas/fixtures/wifi-observations.json). It counts nothing: telemetry counts the tick per router room.

- Which APs: the router sensors placed in the twin, read from GET /telemetry/collector at start and every syncIntervalS (300 s). A router that stays keeps its session; telemetry unreachable keeps the previous list.
- How to reach them: the sensor’s endpoint is the ubus URL (endpointTemplate fills a missing one); driver openwrt-iwinfo selects the iwinfo reader, anything else hostapd.
- What it reports: the routers that answered, every connected phone each one lists (roam leftovers dropped), and the probe bursts. Every tick is posted, even one where no router answered: an empty answered tells telemetry nothing was measured, so no room gets a fresh 0. Trimmed to the contract’s limits (2000 rows, keeping the loudest; 2000 bursts, keeping the newest; 6 loudest routers per burst), since telemetry refuses an oversized tick whole. A refused or failed post is dropped, never retried: the next poll supersedes it.
- How to log in: the collector’s own file — one site-wide ubus login and ifaces, per-router overrides. Never sent to the platform.
- How it proves which building it is: keys: { "<buildingId>": "<device key>" } in the same file, issued by an editor (POST /telemetry/device-keys/buildings/{id}). Each key reads that building’s routers and signs its ticks; it cannot sign for another building.
- Probes (subscribeProbes: true): one hostapd probe stream per router interface, grouped each tick into bursts (app/bursts.py) — one address within 2 s of its first frame is one scan, keeping each router’s loudest frame. A burst the tick cuts in half waits for the next tick. --dry-run prints counts, never an address or a token.
- Tokens (app/tokens.py): every address is swapped for a random token (secrets.token_hex(8)), minted, never derived, so nothing can turn one back. A connected phone keeps its token until it is missing for 3 ticks; a burst gets a fresh one, unless it was sent from a connected phone’s own address. The mac → token table lives only in the collector’s memory.

On OpenWrt the readings come from hostapd over ubus — hostapd.<iface> get_clients returns every associated station with its signal in dBm. iw dev <iface> station dump is the equivalent without ubus.

Per tick:

1. Collect (mac, rssi, idle) from every AP. iwinfo’s inactive is the idle time. hostapd has none: idle is how long that station’s packets.rx has not changed, so it is one poll coarse, and a station first seen counts as fresh.
2. Drop roam leftovers. A MAC listed by several APs keeps only its least-idle rows (within 1 s: each AP is polled on its own clock read). A station associates with one AP; the old one still lists it, signal frozen, until ap_max_inactivity (300 s).
3. Tokenise: swap every MAC for its token; group probes into bursts.
4. Post the tick. Telemetry then counts it: one token is one phone, counted once, in its loudest router’s room.

Union by phone, never sum per-AP client counts
-----
Summing the client lists of overlapping APs is a straight multiplication of the count, and it produces exactly the symptom people expect from MAC randomization. One token on two rows is one phone; telemetry counts it once (kernel/observations.rs).

Smoothing lives in the twin, transitions are not built

Telemetry keeps no state between ticks, so its router-room count can flip a phone between rooms each tick. Digital-twin’s tracks carry each phone across ticks, which is what smooths the dots and estimatedOccupancy. Transition counts (zoneTransition, below) are still not built.

-----

The Platform Side

Occupancy is three metrics, not one

Telemetry stores these for every room, every tick (the factor rides on the tick as devicesPerPerson):

totalDeviceCountratioDeviceCountestimatedOccupancyMetricDevices connected, each in its loudest router’s room. A measurement.Devices ÷ the site’s devices-per-person factor. An estimate.Connected devices placed in the room by position. An estimate.What it istelemetry, from the ticktelemetry, from the tickdigital-twin, Kafka estimated-occupancyFrom

estimatedOccupancy is never mixed into totalDeviceCount: the two place a phone differently, and a dashboard can show both. It counts only rooms on a floor with a placed router, and only ticks where a router answered.

Publishing only the estimate would be the smaller change and the wrong one. The factor is a per-building guess that gets re-measured, and an estimate is only as good as the factor it was derived with. Store the raw count and a corrected factor re-derives the whole history; store the estimate alone and every past bucket is permanently wrong by whatever the old factor was off by. The measurement is also the only one of the two that means the same thing in every building, which is what makes cross-site comparison possible at all.

ratioDeviceCount is emitted only where the site actually configured a factor (useDevicesPerPerson). No factor, no estimate — an estimate silently equal to the device count is a claim about people that nobody made.

Both follow the shape of the existing peopleCount plugin (backend/telemetry/src/plugins/people_count.rs): per building and room, non-negative integer, dashboard catalog, twin overlay, agent tool.

A room’s count is its router’s, not the room’s. A router hears devices wherever they stand, across walls and floors, so the reading keyed to its room says “near this router”. The figure that means what it says is the building’s: telemetry sums the rooms at the building’s newest report and serves it at GET /telemetry/connected-devices/buildings/{id}.

One device, three metrics. The access point is what gets registered as a sensor — device kind router in telemetry’s plugins::devices(), which reports all three. Registering it once per metric would count one device three times.

None carries a threshold. A device count is an access-point capacity question, not a facility one — it breaches on a room full of laptops. And the estimates beside it are guesses, so a bound on them fires on the guess as much as on the building. Occupancy alerting stays with peopleCount, which measures people instead of inferring them.

Optional — per-AP client counts

Separate from occupancy, and useful for Wi-Fi capacity planning rather than for the twin: how many stations each AP is carrying. It needs no deduplication, unlike the zone path — a station is associated to exactly one AP at a time, so the per-AP lists cannot double-count the way overlapping RSSI coverage can.

readings is keyed (building_id, room_id, metric, ts) with no AP dimension, and ingest does not validate room_id against building_rooms. So the cheap shape is a distinct metric with the AP name in roomId:

	metric = "apClients", roomId = "ap-lobby-1", value = 14

Zero migration, existing index, existing hourly rollup. The alternative — the AP name as an extra field in payload — stores fine but is not in the rollup’s group by, so it never aggregates, which is the entire point of collecting it. The cost of the cheap shape is that these rows are only distinguishable from real rooms by their metric key; every query is already metric-scoped, so it works, but it is a convention and not a constraint.

Transitions (not built)

Counts of people moving from one room to another. Digital-twin’s tracks now hold the data to derive them; nothing emits them yet. One new plugin, following the same shape:

	static DESCRIPTOR: MetricDescriptor = MetricDescriptor {
	    value_field: "zoneTransition",
	    key: "zoneTransition",
	    label: "Zone Transition",
	    interface_name: "IZoneTransition",
	    unit: Some("people"),
	    fields: &[
	        FieldSpec { name: "buildingId",     kind: NonEmptyString,  required: true },
	        FieldSpec { name: "roomId",         kind: NonEmptyString,  required: true },
	        FieldSpec { name: "fromRoomId",     kind: NonEmptyString,  required: true },
	        FieldSpec { name: "timestamp",      kind: Finite,          required: true },
	        FieldSpec { name: "zoneTransition", kind: NonNegativeInt,  required: true },
	    ],
	};
	static BOUNDS: &[BoundSpec] = &[BoundSpec { key: "maxTransitions", field: "zoneTransition", label: "Zone transitions", unit: None, direction: Above }];

roomId is the destination; fromRoomId is the extra field, so it lands in the stored payload while the columns stay as they are — consistent with Telemetry Storage. One registration line in backend/telemetry/src/main.rs and the metric is live everywhere.

maxTransitions is not decoration: a sudden flow spike across an edge is the signal for an evacuation or an incident, and the alert path is already built.

Registration

devices/, not simulators/. A simulator is a fake you throw away; the collector is the sensor, shipped to every building and running unattended. edge/ would collide with the ingress proxy, which is what “the edge” means everywhere else in this repository.

- ap-collector: "devices/ap-collector" in .moon/workspace.yml.
- An entry in .github/services.json with no image key. ci-gate.yml gates the docker matrix on select(.image and (.ci != false)), so omitting the image skips the build while the tests still run. Do not copy the simulators’ "ci": false — that also drops the package from coverage and from check-workflow-registry.py, and union-by-MAC is the likeliest bug in the design.
- A job in ci-gate.yml using tpl-python-ci.yml, listed in both docker.needs and ci-passed.needs — check-workflow-registry.py fails otherwise.
- moon.yml overrides the inherited test / lint, which shell out to npm. Agent wraps uv in a package.json; this package cannot, because the root .gitignore ignores every package.json. Both overrides use script:, not command: — command: merges with the inherited task’s args and silently runs uv test.
- Python, no runtime dependencies: ubus and /telemetry/observations are both JSON over HTTP, and signing is hmac.new(key, body, sha256). urllib.request covers it.

-----

What Is Built, What Is Open

Built on branch feat/collector-bursts, against ap-simulator only:

Burst grouping, MAC → token, one signed tick per poll (10 s)Tick contractCheck, count per router room, republish to KafkaEstimator, tracks, accuracy testDots to the browserRoom counts by positionPartdevices/ap-collectortwin_schema::WifiObservations, fixtures/wifi-observations.jsontelemetry POST /telemetry/observationsdigital-twin estimator.rs, tracks.rstwin → Redis twin:devices:{id} → socket devices event → twin view, devices modetwin → Kafka estimated-occupancy → telemetry estimatedOccupancyWhere

Open, and only real hardware answers them:

- A walk test on a real OpenWrt site. The simulator’s radio model and scan rates are guesses; the measured accuracy above holds only on them.
- Probe addresses: does a connected phone use one random address per burst (fine) or per frame (breaks grouping)? How often does it scan with the screen off?
- Exit lag: a router lists a departed phone until ap_max_inactivity (300 s). A time limit would fix it, but would also drop phones that are present but asleep.
- Routers with no placement add nothing to positions; a floor with none gets no dots and no estimatedOccupancy.

The risky unknowns are physical, not code: whether signals separate two rooms depends on where the routers are mounted. Measure before tuning.

-----

Phase 2 — Dedicated Sniffers

Only once phase 1 runs in a real building. Adds coverage of devices that never associate.

Raspberry Pi with a dual-band monitor-mode NIC (mt7612u, ath9k), roughly €60 per unit. An ESP32 is €5 but 2.4 GHz only, and modern phones probe heavily on 5 GHz — systematic undercount. Acceptable for a bench prototype, not for a building.

Do not de-randomize. The literature is good — Bleach reports ~99%, vMac and Espresso combine information elements, sequence numbers and RSSI, one IE-attribute method reports 99% precision across 70+ device types — and every one of them is re-identification engineering. It buys accuracy this feature does not need, at the one cost it cannot pay.

Count without identity instead. RateCount (2025) estimates the device count from a provably unbiased closed form over the rate at which probe frames arrive, with an error model. Learning-free: no training set, no per-site model tuning, no MAC ever inspected. The Keio scheme is the same idea — a phone emits a roughly constant probe rate, so the rate scales with the population.

This is simultaneously the lazier engineering and the defensible privacy story.

Practical corrections the estimator needs: channel hopping means only a fraction of frames are heard, so a duty-cycle term; probe rate varies by phone model and screen state.

-----

Deployment Prerequisites

Phase 1 is only correct if the Wi-Fi is configured for it. These are requirements, not recommendations.

One SSID across all APsOne SSID across 2.4 and 5 GHzWPA2-AES or WPA3Every router placed in the twinOne read-only ubus login on the routersRequirementPer-SSID randomization means a second SSID is a second identity for the same phone.Split-band SSIDs are two networks; use band steering. Standard practice regardless.On open networks Apple rotates the private address every 2 weeks. Encryption pins it.A router sensor in its room, at its position in the twin editor, is the AP → room mapping and the estimator’s geometry; the collector reads the list from GET /telemetry/collector. A router with no placement counts in totalDeviceCount but adds nothing to positions; the editor mounts a router given only a room 0.5 m below that room’s ceiling centre.The collector’s own file holds it (per-router overrides where one differs). Logins never reach the platform.Why

-----

Known Error Sources

Multiple devices per personPeople with no deviceVisitors not on the Wi-FiBoundary flappingWalls, antennas, shadowingAmbiguous burstsRoam leftoversAndroid re-randomize on reconnectSourcePhone + laptop + watch = 3 counts, 1 human. Largest error term by far.Undercount.Undercount.A router-room count flips rooms each tick.Signals read weaker than the radio model expects; positions land a room off.A burst fitting two phones joins neither.Old AP lists a roamed device up to 300 s, signal frozen; holds it in its old room.Split identity.EffectA stated conversion factor per building. Cannot be inferred.Inherent. Document the caveat.Phase 2.Twin’s tracks smooth the dots and estimatedOccupancy; totalDeviceCount stays unsmoothed.Grid fit with walls; measured 79.4% right room on simulated data.Dropped on purpose: no phone gets someone else’s path.Least-idle row per MAC wins. Rows still tied, e.g. both unchanged since the collector started, fall back to strongest signal.Non-default per-network option. Rare; ignored.Handling

What is measured is devices; what a facility manager wants is people. That gap is the conversion factor above, and it is why both numbers are published separately rather than one being quietly substituted for the other. The caveat belongs in the user-facing docs too, not only here: ratioDeviceCount and estimatedOccupancy are estimates and read like facts.

The conversion rounds up. One device at a factor of 2.5 is 0.4 of a person, and rounding that to zero reports an occupied room as empty — the one fact the collector otherwise takes care to keep distinct from a genuinely empty zone. An empty zone still converts to 0.

A rejected or unreachable tick POST is logged and dropped, not raised: the run loop calls the post path directly, so an escaping error ends the collector on a single telemetry restart. One lost batch costs one poll interval of resolution; the next tick supersedes it.

Calibration

Every number that depends on the physical world is configuration, per building:

- devices-per-person conversion factor
- poll interval
- the estimator’s radio model (1 m signal, path-loss exponent, wall loss); today ap-simulator’s values
- phase 2: probes-per-device rate, channel-hop duty cycle

None of these are constants. A building full of engineers and a building full of visitors have different device ratios, and no model can see that from the code.

Two numbers are not on that list, because they are ceilings rather than tuning:

- requestTimeoutS <= pollIntervalS (defaults 5 s and 10 s). Holds only because the collector polls every AP of a building concurrently. Polled in sequence a tick would cost the sum of its APs’ timeouts, so enough dark APs would silently slow the real poll rate. One AP’s own interfaces are still read in series, so an AP with many radios and a long timeout is the one case still worth checking by hand.

-----

Alternative — Consume the Vendor Controller

If the building runs Cisco, Aruba or Mist, the controller already computes client positions. Cisco Spaces Location Cloud API returns cartesian (x, y) per floor; Mist is equivalent.

Zero hardware, zero algorithm — but vendor lock-in, and the vendor holds the MAC addresses. That moves the privacy problem rather than removing it, and the platform then depends on a commercial contract. Worth taking where the hardware already exists; not worth designing for.

-----

Prior Art & References

Ordered by how directly it feeds the build. The first group is code to read before writing any; the research groups are there to justify — or overturn — a decision, not to be reimplemented.

Phase 1 — closest existing implementations

Read these first. Every one solves a piece of the collector.

- vjt/openwrt-ha-presence — the closest analogue. Scrapes RSSI from every OpenWrt AP and assigns each device to a room by strongest signal. This is phase 1’s algorithm, already written, at single-home scale.
- awilliams/wifi-presence — Go daemon on the AP itself, subscribing to hostapd’s control interface for client connect/disconnect events rather than polling. Worth reading for the event-driven alternative to a poll loop.
- WiFi Presence Detection for Home Assistant Using OpenWrt — end-to-end walkthrough. Enables the wifi_stations collector in prometheus-node-exporter-lua, then polls /metrics on each AP every 5 s for wifi_station_signal_dbm. The simplest transport for the collector: no ubus auth, no custom ACLs.
- [HOWTO] Reliable WiFi presence for Home Assistant using OpenWrt hostapd events — the practical failure modes of naive presence detection. Read it for what goes wrong, not for the architecture.
- FUjr/homeassistant-openwrt-ubus — working ubus client pulling per-station RSSI, connection quality and which AP interface each device is on.

Phase 1 — the ubus / hostapd surface

- OpenWrt hostapd ubus interface (source) — authoritative definition of get_clients and the rest. The docs lag; the source does not.
- ubus (OpenWrt micro bus architecture) — techref — the JSON-RPC-over-HTTP protocol: session.login for a token, then call with the object and method.
- OnionIoT — ubus tutorial (part 3 covers rpcd) — the clearest walkthrough of exposing and calling ubus methods remotely.
- Easy ubus daemons with rpcd (Freifunk) and ubus service development with rpcd (Zilogic) — needed if the collector ends up running on the AP.
- openwrt-ubus-rpc (PyPI) — Python client that already wraps login and get_hostapd_clients.
- OpenWrt forum — UBUS over HTTP for WiFi presence detection — the ACL file under /usr/share/rpcd/acl.d/ needed to grant hostapd methods to a non-root RPC user. Easy to miss; nothing works without it.
- Home Assistant — OpenWrt (ubus) integration — documents the exact router-side setup (rpcd, uhttpd-mod-ubus, ACL) in user-facing terms.

Trilateration — reference implementations

Circles lost to the grid fit on simulated data (69% vs 95% right room); listed so the comparison is checkable.

- ifindev/indoor-positioning-algorithms — trilateration and min-max in Python over RSSI from four routers.
- dvalenza/Trilateration-Example — minimal three-signal position solve.
- WiFi Trilateration With Three or More Points — the least-squares generalisation, and the path-loss model d = 10 ^ ((Ptx - RSSI) / (10n)) whose exponent n is the per-site calibration that makes this expensive.
- Indoor Positioning and Tracking in a Multi-Level Residential Building Using WiFi (MDPI) — accuracy actually achieved in a real multi-floor building.

Phase 2 — sniffers and probe capture

- schollz/howmanypeoplearearound — counts probe requests over a window via tshark on a monitor-mode adapter. Small, readable, and the direct ancestor of the rate-based approach.
- GiovanniBaccichet/openwrt-multi-sniffer — an OpenWrt AP sniffing probe requests across multiple channels in both 2.4 and 5 GHz. Bridges phase 1 and phase 2 hardware: it may remove the need for separate Pi units entirely.
- fdd4s/wifi-analytics — captures MAC and RSSI from monitor mode; a worked presence-analytics pipeline.
- ETS-PoliTO/esp32-sniffer — reference ESP32 firmware for probe-request capture.
- SensorsIot/Wi-Fi-Sniffer-as-a-Human-detector — companion code to the video below.
- Building an ESP32 packet sniffer (HackMag) — monitor-mode walkthrough, and the 2.4 GHz-only limitation stated plainly.
- Kismet, monitor mode, wardriving on OpenWrt (forum thread) — Kismet is fully passive and handles channel hopping, logging and device tracking already. Viable as the capture layer under a custom estimator.

Phase 3 — device-free CSI sensing

Not planned. Tracked because it removes the identifier problem entirely.

- espressif/esp-csi — official CSI support, including a wifi_sensing_demo for motion and human presence with on-site training.
- ESP32 CSI Toolkit (repo) — extracts CSI from an ESP32 in active or passive mode.
- Wi-ESP CSI Tool — alternative toolkit.
- Awesome-WiFi-CSI-Sensing — curated paper and tooling index. The single best entry point to this field.

Standards and platform behaviour

- Apple — Use private Wi-Fi addresses — fixed vs. rotating, and which networks rotate. The source for the WPA2/WPA3 prerequisite.
- Android — MAC randomization behavior (AOSP) — per-profile persistence rules.
- Android — Implement MAC randomization (AOSP) — derivation of the address from the network profile.
- IEEE 802.11bf: Enabling the Widespread Adoption of Wi-Fi Sensing (NIST) — device-free sensing; active standard since September 2025, chipsets still thin.
- Indoor Positioning with Wi-Fi Location: a survey of 802.11mc/az/bk FTM (arXiv 2509.03901) — accuracy per amendment, and why FTM is client-initiated.

Counting and localization research

- RateCount: Learning-Free Device Counting by Wi-Fi Probe Listening (arXiv 2507.03873) — the phase 2 estimator. Unbiased closed form over probe arrival rate; no training, no MAC inspected.
- MAC address randomization tolerant crowd monitoring (arXiv 2112.02161) — Vision and TrueSight; also uses data and beacon frames, not probes alone.
- Indoor crowd estimation using the number of Wi-Fi probe requests (Keio) — the constant-probe-rate assumption RateCount formalises.
- Signals from the Crowd: Uncovering Social Relationships (IMC 2013) — the origin of large-scale probe analytics, and a blunt demonstration of what this data reveals when it is not aggregated. Read it as a privacy argument.
- MAC Address Anonymization for Crowd Counting (arXiv 2009.09876) — why salted hashing is not anonymisation, with collision-rate requirements.
- MAC address de-randomization for WiFi device counting (ScienceDirect) — the approach deliberately rejected.
- Efficient Association of Wi-Fi Probe Requests under MAC Randomization — vMac (INFOCOM’21) — likewise: state of the art in the direction not taken.

Datasets and simulation

For validating an estimator before any hardware exists.

- CRAWDAD sapienza/probe-requests (IEEE DataPort) — the classic set: four one-shot events of 40 min to 6 h, plus six weeks of fixed capture on a campus.
- Labelled device Wi-Fi probe requests (Mendeley, 2024) — 22 devices in 6 modes each. The only public set where the emitting device is labelled, so it is the only one that can score an estimator’s error.
- Dataset of Wi-Fi Probe Requests (arXiv 2308.04435)
- WiFiSim: simulating Wi-Fi probe requests via AOSP analysis (arXiv 2509.15501) — generate synthetic probe traffic with realistic device behaviour. Useful for testing before a Pi exists, in the same spirit as simulators/.

Videos

Listed by their published title; orientation, not specification.

- #163 Wi-Fi Sniffer as Sensor for Humans — end-to-end build of a probe-request human detector, with the companion repo above.
- Probe Requests: What They Do And How To Save Them — what a probe request contains and how capture works.

Privacy and law

- Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens — WiFi and bluetooth tracking — MACs as indirectly identifying data; conditions for anonymisation; the multiple-location-points rule this design is built around.
- AP fines municipality for Wi-Fi tracking (2021) — enforcement precedent.
- WiFi-Tracking and Retail Analytics under the GDPR (TechGDPR) — legal-basis analysis for exactly this class of system.
- What does the GDPR say about WiFi tracking? (Privacy Company) — why consent is not a workable basis for ambient sensing.

Vendor controller APIs

If the building already runs managed Wi-Fi, the position is computed for you.

- Cisco Spaces Location Cloud API — active client locations, history, map and AP endpoints; cartesian (x, y) per floor.
- Cisco Spaces — access point auto-location — how AP placement is derived; here the twin editor’s router placement plays that role.
- Juniper Mist — adding an AP for location — note the requirement of line of sight to at least two APs.
